# How to inventory every podcast you've been on

Your past interviews can help people learn what you know. This guide brings them into one list so your team can find and use them. Start with your name, known shows, and any list you already have.

**The path:** Name variants → Discovery leads → Verified appearances → One master list.

**Use this when:** A person needs a consolidated verified appearance inventory across podcast and video sources.

## Inputs
- The person’s verified name/variants, known shows, companies and public identity pages.
- Existing inventory and authorized supplied internal records, with private details kept out of public exports.
- Read access to Listen Notes, Podchaser, YouTube and show pages; account/profile changes have separate scope.
- A master sheet, date/scope, verification statuses, content-use rights and next owner.

## First-run prompt

> Merge the supplied and discovered podcast leads into one source-backed appearance inventory. Verify this person’s role, combine mirrors of the same episode, and keep mentions and uncertain identities separate. Record coverage, rights and metric gaps. Prepare a useful reuse queue without inventing appearances, contact permission or ROI.

## Steps
1. Set up one master record per real appearance with title, show, host, date, role, canonical source, platform links, audio/video availability, verification evidence and next use.
2. Search known names and variants in Listen Notes, Podchaser, YouTube, show websites and the person’s site. Record each source/query/date and any access or coverage limits.
3. Use supplied private archives only within the task’s scope. AI search can suggest leads but must retain a real source URL for verification. Do not turn a claimed result count into a confirmed total.
4. Verify that this person actually appeared and in what role. A mention, same-name person or quote repeated by the host is not a guest appearance. Keep uncertain leads in a review queue.
5. Merge directory mirrors, audio/video copies and reuploads of the same episode into one appearance with multiple links. Use show/title/date/participants/content evidence, not title similarity alone. Separate genuinely different appearances even if they share a show.
6. Record source media availability and permitted reuse separately from presence. A verified guest credit does not grant download, editing or advertising rights.
7. Prioritize useful verified material with comparable observed evidence and the real GCT. Top 20% is a method option with an explicit eligible denominator; unavailable engagement is UNKNOWN, not zero and not a fabricated ranking.
8. Keep hosts and collaborators in a sourced relationship list when useful, without inferring friendship or permission to contact them. Do not claim, edit a profile or send outreach merely because it was discovered.
9. Return the deduplicated inventory, source coverage log, verified/rejected/unresolved totals and priority handoff. If monitoring is part of the job, reuse an authorized alert or named review cadence, with the first result checked before claiming it works.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] One master row represents each verified appearance, with preserved platform links.
- [ ] Role/identity evidence separates appearances from mentions and same-name collisions.
- [ ] Source coverage, rights and metric gaps are explicit.
- [ ] Totals reconcile and monitoring/outreach states are truthful.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no real appearances counted.** Listen Notes finds a sample “Alex on Shop Talk” episode. YouTube has the same conversation under a shorter title, and the host site links both. They become one appearance with three links.

A different episode says “Alex once told me…” but has only the host speaking. That is a mention, not a second guest appearance. # How we use Listen Notes to find, track, and repurpose every podcast appearance

A search for your name can find old podcast visits. It can also find people who only mention you. This guide helps you tell the difference and save the useful results.

**The path:** Name query → Search matches → Episode proof → Merged inventory.

**Use this when:** The appearance inventory needs a reproducible Listen Notes discovery pass.

## Inputs
- Verified public name variants, known shows and identity context.
- The master inventory with lead/verified/mention/rejected/unresolved states.
- Listen Notes search access; exports and alerts may require existing paid access or separate purchase scope.
- Search date/filters and a named inventory owner.

## First-run prompt

> Search the supplied name variants on Listen Notes and record query/filter/date coverage. Capture accessible results or use the already-authorized export. Verify actual episode presence, merge duplicates and keep mentions separate. Treat scores and alerts as their actual measured states; do not buy access or invent delivered notifications.

## Steps
1. Prepare each quoted name variant and known show query. Record query, date and filters so another reviewer can repeat the pass.
2. Search Episodes and capture observed counts and accessible rows. Inspect Podcasts separately for hosted shows. A show match, episode match and verified appearance are different units.
3. Save title, show, date, Listen Notes URL, primary episode link and matching context. Export only when the actual feature/access and cost are in scope; otherwise capture the bounded results manually and state any uncollected remainder.
4. Use filters only when they fit the assignment and record them. Do not apply unique-podcast filtering if the goal is every episode, since that can hide multiple appearances on one show.
5. Open source show notes or episode evidence to verify identity and role. Listen Notes does not transcribe or search all audio; available transcript matches are a limited discovery source. A name in one is still only a mention until presence is established.
6. For priority verified rows, record any available Listen Score/percentile with its date as a show-level estimate. It does not prove guest presence, episode views, revenue or a comparable cross-platform rank.
7. Merge verified rows into the master inventory using episode identity and preserve all source links. Reconcile duplicates and review uncertain matches against Podchaser, YouTube or the host page.
8. If clipping is requested, use only a verified permitted source with actual start/end times and save the resulting state. Search completion does not require creating a clip or making a public playlist.
9. If monitoring is authorized and available, create or reuse the exact Listen Alert query, filters and email/RSS receiver. Verify the saved setting and first actual delivery; keep it “configured, first delivery pending” until observed. Return the updated inventory and remaining coverage gaps.

## First-run prompt

Carry out profile/credit changes already authorized, then read back their true moderation state. Merge only verified appearances and do not infer media rights or contact authority.

## Steps
1. Find the existing creator before creating another. Check name, bio, links and actual work to avoid a same-name collision.
2. If claiming is in scope, use the current Claim Profile process and record its verification request state. Current official help describes team verification; do not assume every user must connect X or substitute someone else’s identity.

5. Judge each credit independently. Confirm host, guest, producer or another actual role only where evidence supports it. Reject same-name and mention-only matches in the work list; keep ambiguous items unresolved. Apply platform changes only through the in-scope route.
6. Compare verified missing appearances with the platform. Submit supported missing credits using the correct episode and role, and save the submission reference. A moderation submission must not be counted as already public.
7. Reopen relevant profiles/episode pages after changes. Reconcile actual accepted/removed/pending credits with the before count; distinguish a show-level recurring role from individually verified guest episodes.
8. Sync confirmed appearances and their sources to the master inventory. Preserve pending submissions and unresolved identity separately. Credit visibility does not grant rights to reuse the media.
9. Return the triage log, actual profile state and next owner. A future credit review needs a real agreed trigger; do not promise the profile will grow automatically or send outreach from this task.

# Process videos via MarketScale

An outside editor needs to know what you want the video to do. This guide helps you send a clear brief and check the finished cut. Start with the real source and the result you need.

## Inputs

- The requested length, orientation, destination, captions, branding and deliverable files.
- The tracker, original-source link, review owner and actual publication/distribution scope.

## First-run prompt

> Prepare and carry out the scoped MarketScale edit request using this archive and brief. Confirm the actual workspace controls, avoid duplicate orders, and check the returned media against the source. Keep audio silent. Return the master/captions, request states and any real distribution URLs; do not equate auto-completion with quality review.

## Steps
1. Record why this source uses MarketScale and what is being requested. Keep the original in the project archive; the provider must not hold the only copy.
2. Confirm current workspace controls and the edit service available. Official help currently documents both a brief-form route and a Request edit conversation. Use the interface actually present and record the chosen route rather than inventing buttons.
3. Upload the correct source into its designated folder and select the actual approver. Complete the platform’s upload-approval step within existing authority. Approval into a workspace/feed is not proof of publication on every external channel.
4. Open the media in Media Studio. Start the current Request edit flow and supply the goal, audience, desired cut length/orientation, source facts and exact caption/branding needs. Check supplied brand assets rather than assuming inherited settings are correct.
5. Review the completed brief and submit once when in scope. Save the video/order reference and requested deliverables. If an active edit conversation already exists, continue it instead of making a duplicate order.
6. When the cut returns, compare it with the source: meaning, names, quotes, captions, framing and agreed output. Keep agent playback silent and record any remaining audio-quality review. Use timestamped feedback and the current revision control for actual defects.
7. Record actual state: uploaded, approved into workspace, in editing, edited, revision requested or complete. Provider auto-completion or elapsed time is not evidence that a human approved the quality. Do not promise the provider’s usual turnaround as this job’s guaranteed deadline.
8. Save the finished master and available captions to the Content Library, with source mapping and checked file properties. If a required download or caption artifact is unavailable, keep that specific deliverable pending.
9. Distribute only to the actual channels in the existing scope through their supported publishing tasks. Save real URLs and visibility. A field named Publishing destination in an edit brief is an instruction, not a public distribution receipt.

# Step 1: Upload video to Google Drive and Descript

Your best video is hard to use if no one can find it. This guide puts the source and work copy where your team needs them. Start with the right file and the folder for this job.

**The path:** Source file → Safe archive → Descript work copy → Two checked links.

**Use this when:** A specific raw recording is ready for Process and a tracker row identifies the project.

## Inputs
- The original file, source date, real speaker names, permission to use it, and any access limits.
- The existing Content Library intake folder and tracker. Run [Set up the Content Library](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=set-up-content-library#task-set-up-content-library) if they do not yet exist.
- Write access to the exact Drive folder and Descript project/drive; enough permitted media minutes for this import. Check the actual account rather than requiring Enterprise by default.
- The agreed naming rule, priority, assigned editor, and intended next action.

## First-run prompt

> Use this source file and exact intake row. Check for an existing import, save the original in the approved archive, and prepare the matching Descript work project. Keep previews silent. Return both checked links, duration, access state and any remaining source review; do not mark an unfinished upload done.

## Steps
1. Read the queue and claim one unprocessed row. Follow any real priority; oldest first is a fallback queue rule. Check that another worker has not already imported it.
2. Inspect the source name, format, duration and completeness. Review accessible frames/captions with silent controls. If intelligible speech has not been checked by an authorized reviewer or non-speaker audio analysis, record that pending check; metadata cannot prove it.
3. Keep the original file intact. Use the existing naming convention, such as YYYY-MM-DD-topic-person, on the working copy or archive entry. Record the original filename so the source can still be traced.
4. Check whether the exact file is already in the brand’s 01-Raw folder. If not, upload through Drive’s New/File upload or the supported project route and wait until complete. Compare duration/size and open the stored item.
5. Check archive ownership and access. In My Drive, placing a file in someone else’s folder does not transfer ownership; a shared drive belongs to the organization. Use the project’s actual approved arrangement without broadening sharing.
6. In the correct Descript drive, create or reuse the matching project and import this same source. Wait for the Activity panel to finish. Add the media to the script when transcription/editing is needed; a file merely listed in the project is not a finished composition.
7. Check the composition contains the expected complete duration and visible frames. Keep a source version before later cuts. Verify that the intended next editor can access both the archive and work project.
8. Save both exact links, file identity, import state and any unresolved speech check in the tracker. Mark this intake as picked up once, then hand the record to transcription.

- [ ] The matching Descript work project contains the intended media and has finished importing.
- [ ] Both links, original identity, duration and next editor are recorded once.
- [ ] Playback or speech checks are evidenced or explicitly pending; no silent test is called an audio pass.

# Step 10: Embed source video

Some readers want to see the person behind the words. This guide adds the real source video to your article. Start with the correct video and the page’s current editor.

**The path:** Verified video → Supported page embed → Caption and layout checks → Source links.

**Use this when:** A video-based article has an embeddable source and needs an actual playable player in the supported page source.

## Inputs
- The actual source video ID/URL, host/channel, rights and intended visibility.
- The article’s canonical record and supported editor or builder source, plus existing embed if present.
- Available captions/language, source context and the content tracker linking the assets.
- Already-authorized edit/publication scope and the next proofreader.

## First-run prompt

> Embed the exact authorized source video in the page’s supported editor or builder. Preserve its URL and source type. Use the actual caption/default policy, no autoplay, and silent player checks. Verify phone/desktop layout and record which reciprocal links and public states are actually complete.

## Steps
1. Verify the source video matches the article and its host allows embedding at the intended visitor visibility. Prefer the brand’s own hosted source when available and appropriate, but an original third-party interview can be embedded with permission; do not reupload someone else’s media merely to make the channel ours.
2. If hosting is needed, hand the actual source and scope to [Upload the video to YouTube](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=upload-processed-video-to-youtube#task-upload-processed-video-to-youtube). Keep this embed pending until a suitable host/player is available. Upload visibility and public article publication are distinct decisions.
3. Inspect the current page source. Use its supported block, builder or existing component; preserve the canonical Page/builder and URL. Do not convert it to Gutenberg solely because a legacy task demanded it.
4. Place the real player near the introduction or section it supports and add short context naming the speaker and lesson. A watch link, thumbnail or transcript panel alone is not an embedded player.
5. Apply [YouTube captions by default](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=enable-youtube-captions-by-default#task-enable-youtube-captions-by-default) through the existing supported helper/filter or explicit embed. Use the verified ID and page language, privacy-enhanced host where supported, cc_load_policy=1, cc_lang_pref, rel=0 and autoplay=0. rel=0 limits related videos to the same channel; it does not disable all suggestions.
6. Check that actual captions exist. The default parameter cannot create a missing track. Keep agent previews muted at volume zero; inspect player state, captions and frames without claiming audio playback.
7. Check actual desktop and phone layout, aspect ratio and initial visible content. Do not assume generic lazy-loading behavior; a lead asset that remains hidden or empty fails. Preserve the source’s portrait/landscape shape.
8. Connect article and video in the tracker. Add a live article link to an editable authorized video description when available; otherwise note that reciprocal edit as pending. Do not claim control of a third-party description.
9. Save through the supported route, record actual preview/public state and hand source/player evidence to proofreading. A draft embed check is not proof that the public canonical page has updated.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The actual source player matches the article and has permitted use/visibility.
- [ ] Existing supported page/builder source and URL are preserved.
- [ ] Caption defaults and actual track availability are distinguished; no first-load autoplay is added.
- [ ] Phone/desktop layout and actual cross-link state are recorded without a false public or audio pass.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no real video ID or embed.** The sample repair-quote article has a six-minute source hosted by the shop. The editor records the real ID from that project, places its player after the short opening and captions the context: “The mechanic shows the three details that help us prepare.”

If the article is still a draft, the tracker says “player verified in draft; public article link pending.” If a permitted interview is on the host’s channel, the editor embeds that original and records that the host controls its description. Neither case justifies a copied upload or a made-up video ID.

# Step 11: Proofread with Grammarly or ChatGPT

Small errors can make a good article hard to trust. This guide helps you fix the words and check the facts before the next step. Start with the full draft and the source it came from.

**The path:** Complete draft → Suggested fixes → Source and voice check → Ready draft or clear gaps.

**Use this when:** The article has its planned text, links, visuals and source player and needs the final Process proofreading pass.

## Inputs
- The complete versioned draft, [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief, verified transcript and source proof.
- The actual spelling/identity list for this project, not a generic list of unrelated client names.
- An approved proofreading tool or manual workflow, with permission to send the draft’s data to that tool.
- The title/headings/search fields, link and media evidence, and next publisher.

## First-run prompt

> Proofread this full draft against the supplied source and project spelling list. Propose small fixes, review each for meaning and voice, and check facts separately. Keep media and text-to-speech silent. Return the corrected revision, key decisions and any unresolved evidence; do not call the article ready from a grammar score alone.

## Steps
1. Save the current draft so each change can be reviewed. If using Grammarly or ChatGPT, request suggestions for grammar, clarity and consistency only. Do not upload private content to an unapproved service or ask for fabricated expansion.
2. Review changes individually. Accept a typo fix or shorter clear sentence; reject a rewrite that changes voice, certainty, chronology, attribution or the actual lesson. Do not bulk-accept every suggestion.
3. Check every name, number, quote and material factual claim against the source or cited primary research. A fluent rewrite is not a fact check. Preserve unresolved claims as explicit editorial gaps rather than guessing.
4. Compare several representative passages with the source voice, including the opening and a direct quote. Ensure personal first person belongs to the real author and company/reference voice remains appropriate.
5. Read the full text in order, including captions, headings and link anchors. Check for repeated words, missing context, abrupt transitions and broken formatting. Use a silent read; do not start text-to-speech through the user’s speakers.
6. Recheck the specific GCT opening and plain first-use term explanations. Use a readability screen to find long sentences, then judge clarity. Keep the meaningful lead visual and page-role requirements intact.
7. Verify that title and description still match the final body and headings remain logical. Google does not impose hard 60/160-character rules, and an exact keyword in the first paragraph is not this proofreading pass’s universal acceptance test.
8. Review the whole-page checklist state. Mark Process ready only for the checked revision and completed applicable work. Keep an unavailable caption/source fact or unresolved rights issue as a specific handoff gap.
9. Save the corrected draft, change notes and evidence references. Hand it to the publisher with the actual scope: draft placement, update or publication already authorized for that job.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Each accepted change preserves meaning, attribution and real voice.
- [ ] Material facts and proper names are source-checked or clearly unresolved.
- [ ] The full draft, captions/headings and first-use terms have been read.
- [ ] The exact final revision and applicable ready/pending checks are recorded without invented SEO or audio guarantees.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no actual draft was reviewed.** A proofreading tool changes “The photo helps us prepare” to “The photo lets us diagnose the fault.” The editor rejects it because the sample source requires an inspection.

The editor accepts “bring you bike” → “bring your bike.” They retain the mechanic’s plain phrase “show us what happens” instead of “provide a comprehensive operational demonstration.” The review note lists those decisions and keeps an unclear source term at 02:18 pending. Better grammar does not erase that evidence gap.

# Step 2: Transcribe video using Descript

A wrong word can change your whole story. This guide helps you turn a video into text you can trust. Start with the full source and a list of the people who speak.

**The path:** Full source → Draft transcript → Word and speaker checks → Verified text or clear gaps.

**Use this when:** The source is imported into the correct Descript project and needs a faithful transcript.

## Inputs
- The completed source composition from [Step 1](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript#task-step-1-upload-video-to-google-drive-and-descript) and access to the original recording.
- A Descript role and usage balance that permit transcription for the source language; confirm actual plan support rather than assuming an Enterprise subscription.
- Verified names, companies, places and specialist terms from project records, plus known speaker identities.
- A place to save the original transcript, corrections, unclear timestamps and review coverage.

## First-run prompt

> Make or review the transcript for this exact source. Use text-correction mode, preserve the media, and check speaker names, numbers and negatives. Keep source versions and timestamp every uncertainty. Report actual review coverage; never call blue-underlined words a complete error list or claim an audio review you did not perform.

## Steps
1. Confirm the source is in the script and select the correct language when transcription is requested. Let the job finish. Check whether a transcript already exists before consuming usage again.
2. Save the initial transcript as a source version. Identify each speaker from actual evidence. If identity is unknown, mark it unresolved in the working transcript; do not assign a famous name by guess.
3. Use Descript’s Correct text action for transcription mistakes. Ordinary text deletion can cut the underlying video; correction mode fixes the words without making that media edit.
4. Check names, numbers, negatives and technical terms against the source. Use the verified spelling list for identity, but do not replace a different spoken person merely because a familiar name is in that list.
5. Review the whole recording and transcript with an authorized speech-review method. Agents keep speaker output muted; if no suitable silent audio analysis or prior reviewer evidence exists, retain the exact unverified intervals for that review. Do not claim a listen-through from a skim or frames.
6. Do not use blue underlines as an accuracy score: current Descript uses light-blue marks for fillers and also has separate alignment/error indicators. Check unmarked words too. Mark unclear speech with its timestamp instead of inventing a clean sentence.
7. Keep this transcript faithful to the recording. Put later summary, grammar edits and filler cuts in a separate working version. Do not generate replacement speech to make an uncertain quote sound correct.
8. Save the checked version with source ID, language, speaker map, review coverage and remaining uncertainties. Only label it verified to the extent supported, then send it to GCT review.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The transcript covers the full source with correct language and evidence-backed speaker labels.
- [ ] Names, numbers, negatives and quotations are checked against the recording, with unclear spans flagged.
- [ ] Text corrections have not silently changed the source media.
- [ ] Review coverage and remaining gaps are recorded; zero colored underlines is not the acceptance test.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no transcript was processed.** The sample audio says, “We do not give a final quote from one photo.” The draft transcript drops “not.” The reviewer restores that word with Correct text and keeps the source video unchanged.

At 02:18, “gear hanger” is unclear. The working row records `02:18 — term unresolved; ask source reviewer`, rather than silently changing it to a familiar part. # Step 3: Watch video and identify GCT

A video can cover more than one point. This guide helps you choose the point your reader needs and the result you want. Start by reviewing the full source and the goal for this job.

**The path:** Whole source → Business goal → Supported content → Specific reader.

## Inputs

## First-run prompt

> Review the supplied source and real project goal. Write three plain lines for Goal, Content and Targeting, with source timestamps and a clear article role. Identify the reader’s question and any unsupported promise. State review gaps instead of claiming a full watch from transcript-only evidence.

## Steps
1. Review the whole source for the story, tone, demonstrations and limits. Read captions alongside frames and use authorized speech evidence. Record portions not actually reviewed; a transcript skim cannot be marked “watched in full.”
2. Write the Goal first: the practical result this piece should help the business achieve. Prefer an actual reader action or need, such as helping a customer bring the right information, over an unmeasured promise to rank first.
3. Write Content second: the specific answer, scene or method the recording actually supplies. Attach useful timestamps. Separate a supported lesson from a proposed topic the speaker never covered.
4. Write Targeting third: who needs this answer, their situation, and the words they use for the question. If a funnel stage is useful, explain it plainly as learning, engaging or ready to act; do not make labels substitute for a real audience.
5. Read these three lines together using [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/). If the source does not serve the requested goal, adjust the article scope or flag the need for new source material. Do not force the transcript into a desired claim.
6. Choose the article role: a repeatable task guide, a broader explanation, a source story, or a record of one run. Only a task recipe needs a complete operational contract; a story should not be mislabeled definitive to fill a checklist.
7. Note the main reader question and candidate search phrase naturally. Search intent helps wording; it does not establish search volume or business performance without measured data.
8. Save the three lines, source anchors, role, scope decisions and open questions. Hand the brief to outlining so every section has a clear purpose.

- [ ] Goal, Content and Targeting are three specific, connected statements.
- [ ] The content line is supported by source moments; missing source review is stated.
- [ ] The goal comes from the project and has no invented performance promise.
- [ ] Audience, article role and main question are clear enough to guide the outline.

# Step 4: Research, edit, add timestamps and outline

A clear plan saves you from writing the same point twice. This guide turns your video notes into sections a reader can follow. Start with the source, the reader’s question, and the goal.

**The path:** Checked source → Topic and source map → Time-marked outline → Writing plan.

**Use this when:** The source and GCT brief are ready, and the writer needs a grounded article outline.

## Inputs
- The verified transcript, original source ID/duration, speaker notes and [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief.
- The current site inventory and access to read existing owned guides.
- Current primary sources for changing facts, and a working document separate from the verbatim transcript.
- The article role, intended canonical page, editor and expected deliverable.

## First-run prompt

> Build an outline from the supplied GCT, full source and owned site inventory. Keep the verbatim transcript intact. Map each section to real source times, separate current primary research from speaker claims, and identify the correct topic home. List specific evidence gaps before writing unsupported sections.

## Steps
1. Search the owned site and inventory for the same reader need. Identify whether to update an existing canonical page or write a distinct supporting piece. Record its place in the [SEO Tree](https://blitzmetrics.com/seo-tree/) before creating a rival guide.
2. Review relevant search results to see common questions, but verify technical or factual additions against primary sources. A high ranking answer is not automatically true or a source to copy.
3. Make an editorial copy of the transcript. Remove repetition and unrelated tangents there while preserving the verbatim source. Keep useful scenes and the speaker’s voice; do not cut a limitation that changes a claim.
4. Mark each topic shift against the original media clock. Use source ID plus start/end time, not guessed times derived from word counts. If the edited video has a new clock, label it separately and keep a source-to-cut map.
5. List the proposed H2 sections and any needed H3 subsections in reader order. Attach a source interval to each source-derived point. Reorder for clarity without implying events happened in a different sequence.
6. Place research notes under the relevant heading with URL, checked date and the precise claim supported. Label them as research rather than attributing them to the speaker.
7. Check each section against the goal and reader. For a task recipe, include its starting state, inputs/access, method, measured output, acceptance and handoff. For a story, keep its actual scene and lesson rather than manufacturing task steps.
8. Add planned visual, owned term explanations and useful next links. State any missing proof beside the section it blocks. Save the outline version and give the writer the source map, not only a list of headings.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The primary topic owner and article role are recorded.
- [ ] Every source-derived outline section maps to a real source interval.
- [ ] Research and speaker claims are clearly separate and checked.
- [ ] The original transcript remains intact; missing evidence and visual needs are specific.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — times are invented to teach the format.** The sample quote video yields this outline:

| Section | Source clock | Writing note |
|---|---|---|
| Show the whole bike | 00:40–01:28 | Explain what the full photo reveals. |
| Show the issue up close | 01:29–02:20 | Keep the speaker’s warning about blurry photos. |
| Say when it happens | 03:10–04:05 | Include the difference between a noise at rest and while riding. |
| Know what still needs a visit | 04:06–05:20 | Preserve the inspection limit. |

A proposed section “Prices for every repair” is dropped because neither the source nor checked research provides that information. If a clip later starts at 00:00 in a new cut, the outline still retains the original source clock above.

# Step 5: Write article from transcript

Your article should sound like the person in the video. This guide helps you turn their best points into clear, useful words. Start with the checked source and the plan for the reader.

**The path:** Checked outline → Source-led draft → Proof and voice check → Complete article.

**Use this when:** The GCT brief and timestamped outline are ready for a full source-grounded draft.

## Inputs
- The verified transcript, full source, timestamped outline and source-review gaps.
- The [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief, page role, intended site and real author/speaker relationship.
- Checked research and media rights, exact quotation/identity records, and maintained [Article Guidelines](https://localservicespotlight.com/article-guidelines/).
- A working document, existing canonical page if any, and named editor.

## First-run prompt

> Write the complete article from my checked outline, transcript and research. Preserve the real author’s voice, source limits and page role. Give the reader a clear answer with useful proof and owned term links. Keep every claim traceable and put unresolved evidence in review notes; do not invent stories, quotes, outcomes or keyword rules.

## Steps
1. Write into the outline one section at a time. Start with the answer or scene supported by the source. Do not ask a model to fill a topic with generic facts when the source does not support them.
2. Choose the correct voice. On a personal-brand page, write as that person in first person when the project supports that authorship. A company article may use third person. Do not make an interviewer’s experience become the named author’s first-person claim.
3. Keep useful concrete details and exact numbers with their source anchors. Paraphrase clearly when a sentence is not a verbatim quote. Add researched claims with their actual citation instead of placing them in the speaker’s mouth.
4. Show the moment, not the resume: lead with a specific scene, useful action or lesson before credentials. Names and awards can supply relevant context; avoid a trophy-name paragraph that substitutes famous names for the story. Make relationship language no stronger than the evidence.
5. Place compact proof near the point it supports: a real photo, exact quote, source video or primary record with known identity/context. Keep the internal verification process, private proof IDs, scoring and research notes in the working evidence map unless those systems are the actual topic.
6. Use praise only with an exact named source, relevant role/company or city, and applicable permission. A quote without verified identity, primary source or needed permission remains **HOLD** and stays out of the public draft. Domain or company attribution alone does not establish a named speaker. Narrow an unsupported relationship claim instead of adding defensive boilerplate about it.
7. Write short paragraphs and explain the first meaningful use of a specialist term with a maintained owned guide. State who, why, the first action and the useful outcome in the opening, using grade-5-or-lower language. This is the maintained opening rule for every document. Use the reader’s phrase naturally without forcing an exact keyword into an awkward first sentence.
8. Make each section fulfill its heading. A task recipe must describe the start, inputs/access, ordered work, measurable output, checks and next step. A story or reference page keeps its own role; do not invent completed work to make it look like a recipe.
9. Compare the whole draft with the GCT and source map. Remove unsupported statements, preserve needed legal disclosures, and mark remaining source gaps in review notes. Save the complete draft for titles and headings.

## Opening meaning review

Keep the opening to two or three short sentences at grade 5 or below. It must show the actual reader’s situation, why the subject matters, the useful result, and how this page helps. A source-backed moment or useful finding can lead. Keep its relevant visual in the first screen; check that the body delivers the opening’s promise.

Save the exact opening and artifact revision in the existing run receipt. Have the reviewer quote the words that establish the situation, reason to care, result and method. Record PASS, FAIL or UNKNOWN with reasons and a readability diagnostic. A grade score, keyword, generic audience label or unsupported conversion promise cannot approve meaning. Follow [Step 7: write and review the opening](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-7-write-hook-and-establish-context#task-step-7-write-hook-and-establish-context) and the [maintained opening standard](https://github.com/dennisyu/local-service-spotlight-skills/blob/main/standards/every-article-and-project-starts-with-specific-gct.md).

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Every factual claim and quote has a source; no invented scene, result or testimonial is present.
- [ ] Voice and relationship wording match the actual author and evidence.
- [ ] The opening is clear, sections answer the reader’s need, and the page’s role is preserved.
- [ ] Proof is useful and close to its claim; private internal evidence notes stay outside public prose.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — the shop and statement are invented.** In the sample recording, Maple Cycle’s mechanic says, “One photo helps us start, but I may need to see the bike.” A faithful draft is:

“A photo helps us prepare for your visit. Send one view of the whole bike and one close-up of the issue. I may still need to inspect it before I can give you a final quote.”

The draft rejects “Get an exact price in minutes,” because the sample source says no such thing. On the mechanic’s personal page, “I” can reflect their voice. A company summary can say “The mechanic may need to inspect the bike.” Neither version claims a real customer result.

# Step 6: Write title and headings

A clear title helps the right reader choose your page. Good section names help them find the answer. Start with what the article really teaches, then name that promise in plain words.

**The path:** Real article promise → Clear title → Useful headings → Checked search preview.

**Use this when:** The article body is drafted and needs its visible title, section headings and search description.

## Inputs
- The full draft, [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief and reader’s main question.
- The current site title convention, existing URL/title if updating, and intended author voice.
- The actual WordPress/template title behavior and search-preview tool when available; a character counter is only an editing aid.

## First-run prompt

> Write a truthful title, search description and heading map from this full article and GCT. Use the reader’s words naturally. Treat 60/160 as optional house drafting targets, not Google limits. Check heading promises and the existing template before adding an H1; keep the current canonical URL.

## Steps
1. Read the article and write one sentence stating what it delivers. Reject title options that promise results, speed or certainty the source cannot support.
2. Draft a clear visible title using the reader’s natural words. Keep it concise and distinct from other pages on the site. Do not rename an established URL just because the title improves.
3. Write a search-title version only when the site uses a separate field. The old under-60 rule can serve as a house drafting target, but Google has no fixed title character limit and may choose different title text. Judge the actual preview and meaning.
4. Write a concise meta description that explains the useful answer. The old under-160 target is not a Google limit or a guarantee of what appears; Google may use the page’s own text. Avoid unsupported offers or results.
5. Make each H2 describe the section’s real answer. Use H3 for a true subtopic under that H2. Use natural variants of the question where helpful, without a quota of keywords in headings.
6. Check the visible page structure: one clear article H1 under the site’s publishing standard, logical H2/H3 nesting, and no fake headings made only by bold text. Existing templates can supply the H1, so avoid duplicating it in the body.
7. Read the headings alone like a contents list. Check that each promise is fulfilled in its section and the order makes sense. Preserve useful source-specific detail without clickbait.
8. Save visible title, optional SEO title, description and final heading outline in named fields. Pass them to the hook writer and later search-metadata task with any template preview check still pending.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Title and description accurately represent the article without unproved promises.
- [ ] Headings make a clear, logical map of actual section content.
- [ ] Visible H1 and template behavior are checked or specifically pending.
- [ ] Preview length is treated as a display/editing concern, not a Google ranking requirement.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no page was changed.** For the sample photo checklist, use the title “What photos help with a bike repair quote?” The headings are “Show the whole bike,” “Show the issue up close,” and “Explain when it happens.”

“Exact bike repair prices in five minutes” is rejected because the article cannot deliver that promise. If the template already prints the page title as H1, the article body begins its sections at H2.

# Step 7: Write hook and establish context

Readers need a reason to stay on your page. This guide helps you show who it is for and what they will learn. Start with one true point from the source, then make its value clear.

**The path:** Real source moment → Reader’s need → Plain promise → Lead visual.

**Use this when:** The full draft and title are ready, but the opening needs a clear source-specific hook and context.

## Inputs
- The full article, title, [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief and actual page role.
- The strongest relevant source scene, question or result, with its exact evidence.
- The intended author voice, source identity and planned meaningful first-screen visual.

## First-run prompt

> Rewrite only the opening from this source, title and GCT. Give the reader a true specific point, who this helps and what they can do next in two or three plain sentences. Add a meaningful lead-visual plan. Preserve actual voice and evidence; do not invent a result or force a keyword.

## Steps
1. Choose the true source moment that best connects to the reader’s problem. A precise question or lesson can lead when there is no dramatic story. Do not manufacture a surprising number to create a hook.
2. Draft two or three short opening sentences that explain who this helps, what the piece covers and the practical result. Make the specific GCT understandable without requiring readers to know the abbreviation.
3. Match the real author voice. Use first person for a supported personal-brand story, or the appropriate company/reference voice. Establish relevant experience through the source scene, not a stack of employers or famous names.
4. Keep the title’s promise honest. A source showing how to prepare for a quote does not support a hook promising a guaranteed price. Explain necessary limits in plain language where they matter.
5. Use the reader’s topic words naturally. Do not force an exact keyword string into the first sentence when it makes the opening hard to read. Explain a new specialist term at first use and link the maintained owned explanation.
6. Place the topic-specific picture, diagram or actual source player where it can be meaningful in the first desktop and phone screen. The visual may lead; a large empty box, tiny text or hidden iframe is not a hook.
7. Read the opening for jargon, long clauses and generic filler. Screen every document opening at grade 5 or below. State the value, audience, first action and useful result in plain words. A formula helps flag problems but does not replace human clarity review.
8. Compare the opening with the source, GCT and next section. Remove resume-style claims and defensive verification language. Retain a materially required disclosure close to its claim. Save the opening with the source anchor and visual placement note.

## Opening meaning review

Keep the opening to two or three short sentences at grade 5 or below. It must show the actual reader’s situation, why the subject matters, the useful result, and how this page helps. A source-backed moment or useful finding can lead. Keep its relevant visual in the first screen; check that the body delivers the opening’s promise.

Save the exact opening and artifact revision in the existing run receipt. Have the reviewer quote the words that establish the situation, reason to care, result and method. Record PASS, FAIL or UNKNOWN with reasons and a readability diagnostic. A grade score, keyword, generic audience label or unsupported conversion promise cannot approve meaning. Follow [Step 7: write and review the opening](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-7-write-hook-and-establish-context#task-step-7-write-hook-and-establish-context) and the [maintained opening standard](https://github.com/dennisyu/local-service-spotlight-skills/blob/main/standards/every-article-and-project-starts-with-specific-gct.md).

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The same short opening explains the reason to care, useful outcome and supporting mechanism; the body delivers that promise and the existing tracker retains quoted reviewer evidence
- [ ] Relevant authentic visual is useful in the first screen; background and context do not bury it

- [ ] The first two or three sentences make who, what and useful outcome clear.
- [ ] The hook is true to the source and uses the correct voice.
- [ ] Language is plain and first-use terms have useful owned explanations.
- [ ] A meaningful lead visual is planned and later rendered checks are explicitly assigned.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no real article or customer claim.** A sample opening reads:

“A blurry bike photo can leave the shop guessing. This guide shows riders which photos and notes help us prepare for a repair quote. Start with a full view of the bike, then show the issue up close.”

A simple three-part diagram below it reads “Whole bike → Close-up → Short note.” It supports the promise without pretending the shop can diagnose every fault from a photo. The writer rejects “Our world-class experts transform your cycling journey” because it gives no useful answer or real scene.

- Money Tree correction, 2026-09-06: replace the vague "A useful conversation becomes a story" orientation with the actual reader value: "Your best customer stories should help your next customer decide to buy. A Money Tree connects those stories, interviews and useful articles to the services you sell, so people can see your work and take the next step." This is a writing example, not a measured conversion result or text to duplicate across unrelated pages.

## Handoff and Content Factory context

The visual editor receives the opening and placement plan for [Step 8: add useful visuals](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-8-add-photos-and-featured-image#task-step-8-add-photos-and-featured-image).

# Step 8: Add photos and featured image

A good picture can make a hard point easy to grasp. This guide helps you choose real proof or a clear diagram for your page. Start with the point you want the reader to see.

**The path:** Point to show → Real source or honest diagram → Clear placement → Phone and desktop check.

## Inputs

- An image editing tool, actual target layout, and a saved original for any resized asset.

## First-run prompt

> Choose and place meaningful source-based visuals for this article. Keep real proof distinct from conceptual diagrams, preserve privacy and image proportions, and write useful alt text. Check the lead at desktop and phone sizes, or record that check as pending. Do not invent photos, results or a guaranteed load time.

## Steps
1. List the points that need a visual explanation or real proof. Prioritize one meaningful asset in the first desktop and phone screen. Add supporting visuals where they improve understanding rather than decorating every heading.
2. Choose a relevant real photo, permitted source-video frame, actual screenshot or evidence-backed diagram. Do not present stock or generated people as the subject or as proof of work. Clearly identify a conceptual diagram as such.
3. Verify who/what is shown and the right to use it. Remove exposed private data from the published copy while keeping the original protected. Do not alter a screenshot to imply a result that was not observed.
4. Select an article-specific featured image. Check existing usage and relevance; retain a suitable canonical image unless the task calls for a replacement. If a new choice is needed, avoid a generic duplicate hero that makes different articles indistinguishable.
5. Crop without cutting off the key person, text or evidence. Resize to the actual display needs and compress while checking legibility. File size alone cannot guarantee a three-second page load; measure the rendered page under stated conditions later.
6. Use a descriptive filename. Give informative images alt text that conveys their purpose. Decorative elements can have empty alt text; do not add keyword-stuffed descriptions or repeat a long caption word for word.
7. Place each asset beside its explanation. Caption real proof with known identity and context, and link the actual source where useful. Keep diagram labels short and readable; preserve image proportions on phone and desktop.
8. Save the draft and inspect the actual layout at 1440×860 and 390×844 when available. Confirm the lead’s meaningful content is visible, not merely its border, and nothing overflows. Record any pending rendered check and give the next editor the asset/source map.

# Step 9: Add internal links with proper anchor text

A reader should not have to search for each new term. This guide helps you add the right link when it is useful. Start with the main topic, then check each person, brand, and idea you name.

**The path:** Named idea → Right owned guide or identity → Clear anchor → Checked destination.

**Use this when:** The article is drafted and illustrated, and its first-use explanations and topic relationships need links.

## Inputs
- The full draft and source evidence for each person, brand and concept.

- Read access to candidate destinations and authorized edit scope for this article or any inbound source page.

## First-run prompt

> Audit first-use terms and named entities in this article. Use the maintained owned guide for explanations and verified identity homes for people and network brands. Keep precise official proof/action links where needed. Check every new path and fragment, use clear anchors, and record actual upward/inbound relationships without forced link quotas.

## Steps
1. List the first meaningful use of each unfamiliar term and named entity. Explain specialist words in plain language before or beside their link. A brand name alone does not tell a novice what the tool does.
2. For a person or managed network business, find the verified identity home. Do not guess a personal domain. For an outside tool or concept being explained, prefer the maintained owned training article; keep official primary proof, sign-in or download links where that specific action or claim needs them.

4. Link the piece up to its relevant topic or task owner and to a useful next guide/action. A source story supports its main guide. Add a service page only where it is a genuine reader next step, not a universal money-page quota for every reference or policy.
5. Use short descriptive anchor words in the sentence. The house guide generally favors three to six words, but a correct named person need not be padded to hit a count. Avoid “click here” and repeated links to the same target in one passage.
6. Check destination scheme, exact path, redirects and any named anchor after #. Confirm a public link does not lead to an unpublished draft or an unrelated homepage. Record access-limited internal links as such when this is internal documentation.
7. Check the inbound path from the main guide or another relevant existing page. Never link a live page to an unpublished/private article as though it were public. Make an authorized inbound edit to the final canonical public target when in scope; otherwise hand the exact sentence and target to that page’s owner. Do not turn catalog adjacency into a prerequisite.

# Use Descript Underlord to remove filler words

Too many stray words can slow a good story. This guide helps you trim them without changing what the person says. Start with a checked transcript and keep a copy of the source cut.

**The path:** Source cut → Review each filler → Selective edits → Checked natural cut.

**Use this when:** A transcribed recording has distracting filler speech and the requested edit includes a cleaner working cut.

## Inputs
- The speaker-labeled source transcript, original recording and a separate editable composition.
- Descript access to the filler tool or Underlord with actual available credits/role; current automatic filler detection supports English.
- The intended tone, source limits and a place to log removed/retained moments.
- An authorized way to review speech quality without playing sound through the user’s speakers.

## First-run prompt

> Review fillers in this separate Descript work copy. Preserve meaningful words and the original source. Choose edit modes deliberately, inspect each boundary, and record removals and retains. Keep speakers silent and state any missing audio-quality review. Do not regenerate the speaker’s words or consume new unapproved tools.

## Steps
1. Keep the original composition and transcript. Create a working copy for filler editing so the factual source is not overwritten.
2. Read representative passages first. Decide whether fillers actually obstruct the message. A natural pause or emotional phrase can be useful; a cleaner waveform is not the goal.
3. Open AI Tools → Remove filler words, or ask Underlord for the equivalent bounded pass on the work copy. Review available usage before consuming it. If the tool cannot support the source language or role, use a reviewed manual edit instead of pretending it ran.
4. Review each detected instance in context. Preserve a real comparison such as “a bike like this.” The detector can flag meaningful words, so do not apply all suggestions blindly.
5. Choose the intended edit behavior. Delete removes text and audio; replace with gap preserves timing. Ignore also removes the audio despite retaining struck text. Remove from transcript leaves the audio in place. Select the operation that actually matches the goal.
6. Use Avoid harsh cuts when available, then check affected boundaries. Restore or loosen a cut that clips a syllable or harms meaning. Do not generate replacement speech as an unnoticed repair to a first-hand source.
7. Review cadence and source accuracy with authorized audio evidence, keeping agent speaker output silent. Frames and captions alone cannot certify natural sound. If that review is unavailable, mark audio-quality review pending and keep the original recoverable.
8. Save the working cut and export/reference it as requested. Log the actual reviewed, removed and intentionally retained instances, output version and remaining checks. Point downstream editors at the correct cut while retaining the original source clock.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The original recording/transcript are retained separately.
- [ ] Every applied removal was reviewed for meaning and the correct edit mode.
- [ ] Speech/cadence review is evidenced or explicitly pending; automatic harsh-cut avoidance is not proof by itself.
- [ ] The final cut, original source mapping and intentional retains are recorded.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no audio was edited.** A sample sentence is “Um, a bike like this needs a close look.” The editor proposes removing the opening “Um” and keeping “like this,” which carries meaning.

At another cut, the start of “needs” is clipped. The editor restores the boundary rather than making a synthetic replacement voice. A sample review log says “2 proposed removals; 1 kept; 1 applied; audio review pending.” It does not say “natural sound passed” from reading the text alone.

# Write email newsletter from video key insight

A short email can share one point your readers can use. This guide helps you turn a video lesson into a clear note. Start with the source, the reader, and the article you want to share.

**The path:** Source insight → Clear email → Checked destination → Draft or verified send.

**Use this when:** A processed video/article has one useful insight for an existing opted-in audience and the job calls for an email draft or send.

## Inputs
- The [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief, full source and checked article or clearly marked draft.
- The real sender/brand voice, email platform, intended list/segment and existing send scope.
- The current template, sender/reply settings, opt-out footer and suppression rules; keep the platform’s existing required controls.
- The campaign history, canonical destination, test recipient when authorized, and measurement owner.

## First-run prompt

> Draft one useful newsletter from this video and GCT in the real sender’s voice. Check the canonical article, intended audience and existing email controls. Complete tests/sends already authorized, then report exact campaign and delivery states. Keep drafts and scheduled sends distinct; do not invent opens, clicks or revenue.

## Steps
1. Choose the single lesson the source supports. State the reader’s useful takeaway before asking them to click. Do not invent a dramatic cost or customer result for the subject line.
2. Draft a few short specific subjects, then choose one that matches the body. Write an opening in the actual sender’s supported voice; company voice need not pretend the sender lived the video speaker’s experience.
3. Deliver the lesson in three to six short paragraphs or a compact list. Preserve the source’s limits and make the email useful even without a click.
4. Add one primary editorial call to action, usually the full owned article. Required footer/opt-out links still remain. Verify the final public canonical URL before a live send; a private draft is not a reader destination.
5. Place the draft into the approved template when in scope. Check names, reply identity, links, images, mobile layout, readable text and existing footer/suppression behavior. Do not change the list or broaden recipients from a previous send by assumption.
6. Send an authorized test to the named test address and inspect the received copy when that step is in scope. A platform preview is useful but not proof of inbox delivery. Keep test and production campaign IDs distinct.
7. Carry out the send or schedule if already authorized after checks pass; otherwise return the complete draft. Record the exact list/segment, chosen time zone, campaign ID and saved state. A scheduled item needs a named first-firing receiver and delivery-state check.
8. Read the platform’s actual post-send results and record sent/accepted, bounced or pending states accurately. A sent-folder copy proves dispatch, not delivery. Later opens and clicks are platform-reported signals, not proof of human reading or revenue.
9. Log the source, article, campaign and observed metrics/date for the existing [Metrics, Analysis, Action review](https://blitzmetrics.com/maa/). Keep unavailable metrics UNKNOWN and give the next owner the specific follow-up.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] One useful source-backed lesson and honest subject are present.
- [ ] Sender, intended audience, footer and final public destination are checked.
- [ ] Draft, preview, test receipt, scheduled and actual send states are distinct.
- [ ] Metrics and handoff use observed evidence without duplicate-send or business-result claims.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no email was sent.** Subject: “Two photos that help before a bike repair visit.”

“A clear photo helps us prepare. Send one view of the whole bike, then one close-up of the issue. Add a short note saying when it happens. We may still need an inspection before a final quote.

See the full photo checklist: `https://maplecycle.example/repair-quote/`.”

The `.example` URL is invented teaching text. A real send needs the actual public article and existing footer. If the test email is received but the campaign is only scheduled, the log says exactly that; it does not report a delivered newsletter.

## First-run prompt

# Maintain a canonical honor and story leaves

You may have a few stories about someone you work with. This guide helps you give them one clear home. Start with the real source and the pages you have.

**The path:** Real shared work → One helpful hub → Distinct story leaves → Checked links both ways.

**Use this when:** New material about a real relationship should improve an existing or justified main honor page and its specific story pages.

## Inputs
- Verified relationship evidence, intended [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) and public/private limits.
- Original recordings/transcripts/photos, media permissions and known identity home.
- An inventory of the existing honor hub, people-directory card and story leaves, with current source revisions.
- Approved site/channel edit scope, source owners and actual next recipient.

## First-run prompt

> Use the real relationship evidence and existing page inventory to improve one canonical honor hub and its distinct stories. Name actual themes, preserve rich URLs, add useful links both ways and verify media/identity. Keep private relationship data out of public copy. Complete only the already-authorized site/distribution actions and record true public or pending states.

## Steps
1. List the existing pages about the relationship and what each does. A people-directory card is not the full honor, and a short person-slug stub does not earn the main role by its URL alone.
2. Choose one helpful canonical relationship page on the relevant site. If it is thin, improve it from real shared work and sources before making claims about its authority. Do not create a competing biography to handle every new recording.
3. Name the real themes or limbs under that hub. Place each distinct tape/story under an appropriate theme. If no theme fits, record the content-placement decision rather than forcing an unrelated story onto the site.
4. Process each useful tape into its own source-faithful story with quotes checked against the transcript. Keep the real scene and lesson; the derivative story is not a second main relationship essay.
5. On each leaf, put the verified source player or meaningful visual early, with the named theme and link to the main hub visible in the first screen. Use the maintained caption/no-autoplay policy and no guessed or known-dead video IDs.
6. Update the hub with a useful summary and inbound link to each leaf under the correct theme. Link the person’s verified entity home. Keep relationship terms proportional to evidence and do not publish private contact data or invented introduction paths.
7. Preserve rich story URLs. Only a true duplicate honor might justify a scoped redirect; do not send a rich story into a thin stub or assume every similar slug should redirect. Verify any authorized redirect’s final target.
8. Save each change through its supported source and check normal canonical desktop/phone views. Reconcile the actual inventory: one hub, named themes, leaf-to-hub and hub-to-leaf links, source IDs and any pending external-site edit.
9. Use only the distribution destinations in the existing plan. Another person’s site or audience is not ours to edit from a relationship claim. If an intake monitor is requested, use a real watermark, duplicate check, quiet no-change path and named first-firing owner; do not install one for every honor page.
10. Write the run’s meta with the actual changed pages, proof and remaining work. Hand the useful public pages or staged changes to the next owner, with promotion reserved for the separate evidence-based scope.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] There is one useful relationship hub and distinct preserved stories, not competing masters.
- [ ] Each leaf names its theme and links the hub early; the hub links the real leaf and entity home.
- [ ] Evidence, media IDs, privacy and relationship wording are verified.
- [ ] The actual save/public state and inventory reconcile; no unasked redirects, outreach or scheduler are inferred.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no real relationship or site edit.** A sample business owner has one page about working with a local mechanic and two stories: a shop visit and a photo-checklist lesson. The main page describes the actual shared work. The visit story remains about that visit; it links up under “Shop visits.” The checklist story links up under “Customer education.”

The hub links both leaves and the mechanic’s verified business home. It does not call the mechanic a partner or friend unless the real evidence supports that wording. No rich story is redirected into the hub merely to reduce the URL count.

# Email and DM client about published article

Your client should not have to hunt for their new article. This guide helps you send the live link and one useful next step. First, check the page and the client’s real contact details.

**The path:** Live page → Right person → Email and short note → Saved follow-through.

**Use this when:** The article is publicly visible and the job includes telling the client it is live. A DM is a direct message in the chat channel you both use.

## Inputs

- The exact client email/thread and normal direct-message channel from the project record. Check identity rather than guessing from search order.
- Existing authority to send on those channels, the approved sending account, and the requested ask. Carry forward permission already given for the job.
- The tracker, current notification history, next owner, and any agreed follow-up cadence.

## First-run prompt

> Use the checked article and exact client thread I provide. Draft a short email and a message with one useful ask. Carry out sends already authorized for this job, then verify each sent copy and log it. Check existing messages before follow-up. Do not claim a send, share, reply, or ad launch without evidence.

## Steps
1. Open the canonical article as a visitor. Confirm the correct title, source, and visible content. A saved WordPress response alone does not prove it is live. Check each social link before including it.
2. Read the exact client thread and tracker. Confirm the recipient and current channel. Check whether another worker already sent this notification; do not create a duplicate.
3. Write an email with a clear subject such as “Your article is live: [title].” Include the article link, two short lines on the useful point, and one specific ask. State only distribution or promotion that actually happened.
4. Prepare a short note for the client’s normal direct-message channel. Link the article or the relevant social post and use a personal, factual sentence. Do not claim a screenshot was taken or praise received unless that is true.
5. Send the email and message when these sends are already in scope. If the job covers only a draft or one channel, finish that authorized work and label the task result draft or partial rather than sent. Do not request duplicate approval for an authorized send.
6. Read back the sent copy in each exact thread. Log date, channel, recipient, sent-message reference, links, and the ask. A composed draft or a send-button click without confirmation is not a sent receipt. A sent-folder copy proves dispatch, not delivery: record a bounce, failed DM, or rejected destination as failed or pending with its next owner.
7. Follow the project’s existing cadence. The source proposes one follow-up after 48 hours with no reply; use it only when that follow-up is part of the agreed job. Check for a real reply and another worker’s recent message before following up.
8. If a reply arrives, record it accurately. A positive private reply can inform a later [Thank You Machine](https://blitzmetrics.com/thank-you-machine/) task; it is not automatically public testimonial permission. Handoff or close the remaining follow-up with its true state.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The canonical article and included social links are actually live.
- [ ] Each in-scope message is confirmed sent to the intended person and recorded once; draft-only, partial, bounced and failed-delivery states are not called a completed notification.
- [ ] The message gives accurate context and one clear ask, with no invented promotion or response.
- [ ] Follow-up has a real owner/state; no reply is recorded as no reply, not failure of the send.
- [ ] Any quoted response retains its privacy and use limits.

**Fictional teaching example — no message was sent.** Maple Cycle’s sample article explains how to ask for a repair quote.

The sample DM is: “Your quote guide is ready to share: `https://maplecycle.example/repair-quote/`. The photo checklist is the part I think riders will use most.”

# Place content on SEO Tree with proper links

A useful page can still be hard to find. This guide helps you connect it to the main topic and the next thing a reader needs. Start by finding the page that already owns that topic.

**The path:** Page’s purpose → Main topic owner → Useful links both ways → Checked map.

**Use this when:** A new or existing piece needs a clear place in the site’s topic map.

## Inputs

- The current [SEO Tree](https://blitzmetrics.com/seo-tree/) map and content inventory, with the agreed main page for each topic.
- The [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief: the result wanted, the content used, and who it serves.
- Access and scope for the page and any related pages to be changed. Record an inbound-link handoff if another site owner must add it.

## First-run prompt

> Use my page, current site map, and authorized edit scope to find its real topic owner. Propose useful links in both directions, read the targets, and check named anchors. Make the already-authorized changes and verify them. Record any inbound edit another owner must make; do not invent a hub or claim a pending link is live.

## Steps
1. Read the piece and classify its role. A specific story or answer usually supports a broader guide; a guide may own a repeatable task. Do not mark a story definitive just because it has links.
2. Search the site inventory for an existing page that already answers the same main need. Enhance the canonical page when appropriate. Record why a distinct supporting page is needed rather than silently making a rival hub.
3. Choose the actual parent topic and any useful next guide. Read the target pages. Resolve each target to its final canonical URL; do not build new body links to a redirecting alias. A category or plugin suggestion is a clue, not proof of the right relationship.
4. Add a body link from the specific piece to its main topic or task guide where the reader needs the explanation. Use descriptive words that match the destination. Add related links only when they help a real next question.
5. Follow the [entity-linking guide](https://blitzmetrics.com/entity-linking/): use verified identity pages for people and managed brands, owned explainers for methods and tools, and precise primary sources when they substantiate a claim or needed action. Do not invent a person’s domain.
6. Add a relevant link from the parent or a suitable existing supporting page to the new piece within the authorized edit scope. Do not publish an inbound link from a live page to a private or unpublished target; stage that edit until target visibility is checked. If the edit is outside scope, give the responsible owner the exact sentence, target, and reason; keep inbound placement pending.
7. Save through the site’s supported source. Check each final destination and any fragment after #. Confirm the live body links when publication is in scope; draft links remain draft-only checks.
8. Update the inventory with this page’s role, primary parent, actual inbound source, links, and checked date. If no parent fits, state whether the content or map needs a decision rather than inventing a branch.

- [ ] The role and primary topic owner are stated and source-grounded.

- [ ] New links and named anchors reach the intended content; no unsupported duplicate hub or redirect alias was made.
- [ ] The inventory records the actual placement and verification state.

**Fictional teaching example — no site was edited.** Maple Cycle has a main “Repair quotes” guide and a smaller story, “What happened when a photo missed the bent part.”

The story links up with “how our repair quotes work.” The guide links down with “a quote changed after inspection” beside the section explaining why photos are only a starting point. A booking page is linked where the reader is ready to arrange a visit.

The sample map is `Repair quotes guide ↔ inspection story → booking step`. It does not link every page to every other page. If the guide’s editor has not yet saved the inbound link, the story’s inventory row says “upward link checked; inbound edit pending,” not “fully connected.”
