# Post to Facebook page

Your page can help customers find a useful answer. This guide shows you how to share a clear post from the right business. Start with the real article or clip and one point worth sharing.

**The path:** Approved source → Correct Page → Clear post → Live link and comments.

**Use this when:** The distribution plan calls for a post on a specific Facebook Page and the source is ready.

## Inputs
- The exact Facebook Page, approved posting scope and access to create its content. Facebook access and task access are different; task access may use Meta Business Suite.
- The checked article URL and/or finished media, rights, source facts, caption notes, and intended audience.
- The real voice and attribution of the speaker or business. First person must refer to a real supported speaker, not a fabricated personal experience.
- The content tracker, current posting history, named comment owner, and a named receiver for any scheduled-post check.

## First-run prompt

> Use the exact Page and source I provide to prepare a short factual post. Check the current posting history and media rights. Publish, schedule, or save only as already requested, verify the resulting state, and log the direct link. Do not start ads or claim reach from a post existing.

## Steps
1. Open the specified Page or its Meta Business Suite workspace. Verify the selected business and account identity before creating anything. Use the existing approved route; possession of a token alone is not a posting instruction.
2. Check the recent content list for the same article or clip so retries do not create duplicate posts. Confirm the article is publicly readable if the caption says it is live.
3. Write two to four short sentences: the real question or point, one supported takeaway, and a helpful next step. Keep the wording true to the actual speaker. Use the owner’s first person only where the source and assignment support it.
4. Open the create-post composer for that Page. Add the caption and the selected real photo or video. Choose the available media/post format shown by the Page. Native media is an editorial choice, not a promise of higher reach.
5. Include the specific article link where readers can find it. If the plan uses a first comment, that comment is part of the handoff and must actually be added and checked. Tag only confirmed featured people or Pages when the mention is relevant and available.
6. Preview the source, crop, text, link, and selected destinations. Add accurate photo alt text or usable video captions where the composer supports them; otherwise record the accessibility limit. Keep any media preview muted at volume zero. Publish when already authorized, or save the in-scope draft/scheduled post. Do not add a boost, spend, or another platform just because the composer offers it.
7. Open the resulting post as the intended viewer where possible. Check the Page name, caption, media, link, and mentions. Copy its direct URL and record the observed status and time. For a scheduled item, give a named receiver the scheduled time and timezone; that receiver checks the first firing and public URL after the due time.
8. Hand a verified live post to [Engage with social comments](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=engage-with-social-comments#task-engage-with-social-comments) under the agreed response scope. A scheduled or failed item stays with its firing-check receiver until its public state is known. Later measurement can inform [the Facebook boost shortlist](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=boost-top-3-5-facebook-posts#task-boost-top-3-5-facebook-posts); a Page post is not automatically eligible or approved for an ad.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The post belongs to the specified Page and has the intended draft/scheduled/live state; scheduled is not called live and has a named first-firing receiver.
- [ ] The caption and media match the actual source and rights; accessibility support or its exact limitation is recorded, with no unsupported reach claim or personal story.
- [ ] The article link and intended mentions work, or a specific limitation is recorded.
- [ ] The direct URL, time, channel, and correct next owner for the current state are saved once.
- [ ] No ad spend or extra distribution is implied by the organic post.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no Facebook post exists.** Maple Cycle’s sample caption reads:

“Not sure what to send us for a repair quote? A clear photo and a short note about the problem help us plan the next step. Our guide explains what a photo can tell us and what needs a shop visit: `https://maplecycle.example/repair-quote/`.”

The planned image is the shop owner beside an actual workbench. In a real run it must be the real authorized photo. If the post is scheduled for tomorrow, the tracker must say “scheduled,” not “live.” This invented post supplies no engagement or boost evidence.

- An existing WordPress user that represents that person, with correct public name and approved profile details.
- Permission to edit the scoped article author, and separate user/profile access if those details need changes. A new user is not automatically required.

## First-run prompt

> Use the exact post list and confirmed author mapping I provide. Check the current values, make only the already-authorized author changes, and compare the saved record with the public byline. Preserve other fields and guest credit. Report template or identity gaps without sweeping unrelated posts.

## Steps
1. Read the article and assignment. Confirm who is responsible for the published voice. Follow [Article Guidelines](https://localservicespotlight.com/article-guidelines/) for personal-brand first person; do not reassign a genuine guest’s work to a site owner merely to remove an admin-looking name.
2. Find the existing user record. Match the actual person using more than a similar name. Check the public display name, approved bio and photo. Keep login identity and public byline separate.
3. Open the exact post’s settings and select the correct author. Use the supported site editor or publishing tool. A REST route is suitable only when it is already the approved source path for that site and content type.

5. Open the public article after an authorized update. Check the visible byline and any author box. A template may show a custom byline that differs from the stored author; correct the actual supported source rather than pretending the data change fixed the display.

# Share in 44K Facebook group

A group post should give people something they can use. This guide helps you share a lesson from a real article. Start by checking the right group and its current posting rules.

**The path:** Correct group → Useful lesson → Submit and check → Replies and evidence.

**Use this when:** The distribution plan names a specific group and the checked article is ready for that audience.

## Inputs
- The exact group URL/ID and current rules. “44K” is the legacy task name, not a verified current member count or enough information to identify the group.
- The checked article, source facts, real media, and identities of any members to mention.
- The authorized posting identity, actual ability to post in the group, and the job’s message/publication scope.
- The distribution tracker, client-notification state when required by the plan, and a named person for comments and measurement.

## First-run prompt

> Use the exact group and article in the plan. Check group rules, posting identity and duplicate history. Share the useful lesson already authorized, then record whether it is pending or live. Keep replies and later measurements truthful; do not assume group size, reach, or boost eligibility.

## Steps
1. Open the exact group and read its current rules. Verify that the planned identity can post and that links, media, and this kind of content are allowed. Group membership does not guarantee immediate posting rights.
2. Read recent group posts and the tracker for duplicates. If the plan requires client notice first, verify that notification rather than assuming it from a checklist neighbor.
3. Write a short lesson: the problem, one supported detail, and what another member can do with it. Link the full article only when the current group rules allow that link. If links are barred, use a useful native lesson when it still meets the approved distribution goal; otherwise hold the post and name the rule conflict. Do not force a number into the post when the source has none.
4. Add a relevant real photo or clip if allowed and useful. Add accurate photo alt text or usable video captions where the group composer supports them; otherwise record the accessibility limit. Mention only confirmed featured members when appropriate. Keep media previews muted; no invented banner result or testimonial belongs in the post.
5. Submit when the job already authorizes posting. Read the resulting state: published, waiting for admin approval, rejected, or failed. Record the post/submission reference. Do not resubmit a pending item to force it through.
6. When live, confirm the text, link, identity, and media in the group. Restricted group content may require a member view; do not claim anonymous public access or general visibility.

# Step 12: Post article on WordPress

A finished draft needs a clear home on the site. This guide helps you put the words, pictures, and video in the right place. Start by checking whether the page already exists, so you can keep its links and history.

**The path:** Prepared article → Correct source record → Layout and checks → Saved or published state.

## Inputs

- Access to the supported editor or publishing tool. For an existing Page or builder, identify its real save source and preserve it.
- The media files, approved destination paths, previous revision, and next publisher/reviewer.

## First-run prompt

Complete the already-authorized save or publication. Verify saved data and normal visitor content separately, and report the exact remaining issue.

## Steps
1. Search the site and inventory for the canonical page. Update that record when it already owns the topic. For a genuinely new editorial guide, use a Post and the block editor where appropriate. Preserve an existing Page, builder, URL and supported source; do not rebuild it solely to fit this task.
2. Save the current source and key fields before an update. Check again before saving so a newer edit is not overwritten. Keep the title, date, author and URL unchanged unless the work explicitly calls for changes.
3. Place the article in the supported editor. Use one visible H1, clear H2/H3 sections, short paragraphs, and the real speaker’s voice. Confirm the opening says who it helps, why, and the useful result in plain language.
4. Place the article-specific visual early enough to work in the first desktop and phone screen. Add the real media with descriptive alt text and source/permission notes. A hidden featured-image setting or empty colored box does not meet the visual rule.
5. Embed the actual source video when the article depends on it. Use [YouTube captions by default](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=enable-youtube-captions-by-default#task-enable-youtube-captions-by-default) for the player settings. Keep previews silent; a pasted watch URL, poster alone, or transcript pane is not the finished player.
6. Verify the pasted body links and named anchors using [entity-linking guide](https://blitzmetrics.com/entity-linking/). Keep owned teaching links, accurate identity destinations, and specific primary proof. For new content, choose a clear stable slug; do not change an established URL just to fit a keyword.
7. Save a draft when the job is staging work. Complete [categories and tags](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-13-categorize-post-and-add-tags#task-step-13-categorize-post-and-add-tags), [search metadata](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-14a-configure-rankmath-seo-plugin#task-step-14a-configure-rankmath-seo-plugin), author and link checks as applicable, then run [Check the full article checklist](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=verify-all-items-on-blog-posting-checklist#task-verify-all-items-on-blog-posting-checklist). A plugin step is not a reason to replace an existing supported builder.
8. If publication/update is already authorized and applicable checks pass, publish through the supported route without asking again. Read back the saved record, then open the normal public URL on desktop and phone. If an approved cache/static publishing step is needed, use the maintained procedure and verify the served result.
9. Log the exact record, revision, saved state, public URL, visual checks and any pending publication layer. A draft preview, successful API response, or cache-busted copy alone is not proof that ordinary visitors see the change.

- [ ] The article structure, source facts, media and links survive the transfer.

- [ ] Saved draft/published state matches the job, with no unasked URL or content-type change.

# Step 13: Categorize post and add tags

Good labels help people find more useful work on your site. This guide helps you choose the right topic group and tags for a post. Start with the site’s own list, so you do not create two names for the same thing.

**The path:** Page purpose → Existing labels → Saved category and tags → Checked grouping.

**Use this when:** A WordPress post needs its category and tag labels set or corrected.

## Inputs
- The exact post, its [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief and its place on the [SEO Tree](https://blitzmetrics.com/seo-tree/).
- The site’s current category/tag list and rules. A category groups related posts; a tag is a reusable label across posts.
- Permission to edit this post’s labels; scope for new terms if the existing list truly lacks a needed one.
- The content inventory, publication state, current canonical URL and permalink policy. Pages may not use post categories/tags unless the site explicitly adds that support.

## First-run prompt

> Use the exact post and current site taxonomy I provide. Select the right existing category and useful tags, save the authorized change, and verify the saved values. Keep draft and public archive checks separate. Do not create duplicate tags or add an internal stage system the site does not use.

## Steps
1. Read the post’s main purpose and current topic map. Identify the existing category that fits. A category archive and a maintained topic guide may be different pages; record both rather than assuming the category is the guide.
2. Open the post settings and Categories panel. Choose the agreed main category. Use a second only where the site policy and content support it. One primary category is a house choice; WordPress itself permits more than one.
3. Remove an accidental default “Uncategorized” assignment when a correct category is now set, within this post’s scope. Do not rename or delete the site’s global default category as part of a one-post task.
4. Open Tags and reuse exact existing terms. Choose only labels that help navigation or an established workflow. Stage tags, format tags, people and company names are not mandatory on every public site; do not invent them from an old template.
5. Review near-duplicates before creating a new tag. For example, “repair quotes” and “repair-quote” may point to the same idea. If the taxonomy needs a new term, follow the already-authorized taxonomy scope or record the specific missing decision.
6. Save the post in its intended state. Reopen its settings and confirm the actual assigned terms. Compare the canonical URL before and after because category-based permalink setups can change a public address; restore the scoped value or hold the result if the URL moved unexpectedly. If a machine lookup is part of the job, test the supported category/tag query with the correct IDs and access; do not assume every custom type exposes them.
7. For a published post, check its intended archive, visible labels and normal canonical URL. For a draft, inspect the archive’s existing siblings and the saved term assignment, but do not expect the unpublished post to appear publicly.
8. Update the inventory with the category/tag names or IDs, URL result and any justified not-applicable fields. Hand the record to [Configure search metadata](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-14a-configure-rankmath-seo-plugin#task-step-14a-configure-rankmath-seo-plugin).

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The category fits the post’s actual topic and the site’s current structure.
- [ ] Tags reuse useful existing terms; no duplicate or invented workflow taxonomy was added.
- [ ] Saved terms match the plan and the supported content type, with no unasked canonical URL change.
- [ ] Published archive behavior and canonical URL are checked only when applicable; draft status is not treated as an archive failure.
- [ ] The inventory records exact labels, URL state and any unresolved term decision.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example — no taxonomy was edited.** Maple Cycle’s sample post answers “Can a photo get me a repair quote?” The site already uses category “Repair quotes” and tag “Planning a visit.”

The publisher selects those terms and rejects a new tag called “repair-quote” because it adds no useful distinction. The draft saves with both term IDs. It does not show in the public archive yet, which is expected for a draft.

# Step 14a: Configure RankMath SEO plugin

People need a clear reason to open your page from search. This guide helps you set its title and short summary. Start with the real question the page answers, then check that the saved words match it.

**The path:** Real search need → Clear title and summary → Plugin checks → Saved output.

**Use this when:** A prepared WordPress article needs its Rank Math search metadata configured or rechecked.

## Inputs
- The exact page/post, target reader, main question or focus phrase, and current [Goals, Content, and Targeting](https://blitzmetrics.com/gct-business-strategy/) brief.
- An existing working Rank Math setup and permission to edit the page’s fields. Rank Math is a WordPress add-on that checks page text and stores search titles and descriptions. Installation, licensing or paid Content AI is not assumed.
- The current page URL and intended canonical URL, which is the main address search engines should treat as the page’s home. Keep the accepted schema (machine-readable page details) and indexing rules with the brief.
- The editorial acceptance target and latest source draft. The legacy task uses score 70+ as an internal target, not a search-ranking guarantee.

## First-run prompt

> Use the article and agreed search need to set clear Rank Math metadata. Check the installed plugin’s actual tests, fix factual issues, and record the measured score. Keep existing URLs and site settings unless their change is already in scope. Verify saved and served output without promising a Google ranking.

## Steps
1. Read the page and choose the phrase that honestly describes its main need. Avoid expanding to unrelated keywords just to raise a score. Check whether an existing page already owns that topic.
2. Open the Rank Math panel. Set the primary focus keyword. This is the phrase the plugin tests; it is not a command to Google to rank the page.
3. Open General → Edit Snippet where available in the installed editor. Write a clear title and a unique description. Use the source’s under-60 and under-160 character aims as editorial guides, then inspect the displayed width. They are not Google’s fixed limits or a guarantee against truncation.
4. Check that the title, opening and useful headings name the subject naturally. Describe images accurately in alt text rather than inserting a keyword that does not fit what the image shows. Keep an established URL unless a separate URL change is justified and authorized.
5. Review the plugin’s actual tests and fix real omissions. The current beginning-of-content test generally checks the first 10%, not a universal first-paragraph rule. Do not add false facts, padded sections, paid AI, or awkward repetition to satisfy a score.
6. Record the measured score and remaining flags. Compare it with the agreed internal target. If sound editorial choices or parser limits keep it below target, state the exact issue for review instead of looping forever or silently claiming a pass.
7. Inspect the snippet preview, canonical URL and schema type against the actual page. Preserve valid site defaults unless this task includes their correction. Do not change global indexing or plugin settings to improve one score.
8. Save and reopen the fields. After an authorized publication/update, inspect the served title, description and canonical output for this URL. Google may choose different title/snippet text; plugin preview and stored metadata are not proof of a search result or ranking.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The focus phrase describes the actual page; title and summary are specific and readable.

# Step 14b: Run LinkWhisper for internal links

A link tool can suggest pages, but it cannot choose your story for you. This guide helps you pick links that make sense. Start with the page’s main topic, then read each suggested target before you add it.

**The path:** Topic map → Review suggestions → Scoped link edits → Saved link checks.

**Use this when:** A prepared article needs useful outgoing and incoming links, and the site uses Link Whisper.

## Inputs

- A working Link Whisper installation, license/features where required, and current link data. Link Whisper is a WordPress add-on that suggests and adds links. Check that its installed version supports the editor and content type.
- Authority and access to change this article and any older pages chosen for incoming links.
- The page’s publication state, current revision and a place to record each source sentence, anchor, target and result.

## First-run prompt

> Review Link Whisper suggestions for the exact article and page map I provide. Read targets and choose useful links; apply only scoped edits. Check older source pages before adding incoming links. Do not enable auto-linking or paid AI by default. Report inserted links separately from suggestions and staged edits.

## Steps
1. Open the existing Link Whisper setup and confirm it is ready for this post type. Verify that its content scan includes the current article revision; run the approved scoped scan or name the setup owner when data is stale or setup is missing. Do not accept launch-wizard defaults blindly: current options may create automatic linking rules.
2. Read the article’s outgoing suggestions. These point from the article to other pages. Open each candidate and compare it with the sentence’s meaning and the main topic owner.
3. Choose a small set of helpful links. Point method mentions to their maintained owned guide; use accurate identity destinations and precise primary proof where needed. Reject irrelevant, duplicate, misleading or competing-hub suggestions.
4. Edit anchors into clear words that describe the target. Follow the maintained house guidance of roughly three to six descriptive words where it fits, without changing the sentence’s meaning to hit a word count.
5. Apply only the reviewed outgoing links through the supported editor/plugin control. Save and check that the expected sentences and URLs survived. If the editor/builder is unsupported, route a manual source-aware linking task and do not claim the plugin succeeded.
6. Review incoming suggestions, which would add a link on an older page pointing here. Confirm each older page is in scope and that the final target will be accessible to its readers. Avoid publishing a public link to a private draft.
7. Apply the specific authorized incoming edits and verify the changed source pages. Record any separate owner’s pending action. Do not turn a single-page link pass into cross-site connection, autolinking, paid AI processing, or a global search-and-replace.
8. Check every added URL and named fragment, first in the saved content and then in the served body when published. Update the inventory with actual outgoing/incoming paths and any pending work. Suggestions or map lines are not proof that links were inserted.

Check both exact first-screen sizes, the full body, links and silent media behavior. Make already-authorized repairs and recheck them. Open the normal canonical URL as an ordinary visitor, not just a draft preview or special cache-busted link. Compare the title, opening, key edited sections and intended CSS/media to the latest accepted revision. A saved WordPress result and served page are separate checks. 2. At 1280×800 and 390×844, inspect the first screen before clicking or scrolling. Capture the meaningful visual, readable labels, title/opening and absence of sideways overflow. A whole image need not fit every long page, but the useful visual content must be visible and understandable under the maintained rule. 3. Scroll through the rendered body. Check headings, paragraph gaps, tables, image aspect ratios and any preserved builder blocks. Keep the voice and identity rules from [Article Guidelines](https://localservicespotlight.com/article-guidelines/). Fix observed layout failures in the actual supported source. 4. Otherwise mark the form action UNKNOWN with its named owner; do not pass it from appearance alone. 5. Check the actual video or hosted source player, caption policy, thumbnails and image descriptions. Keep the player muted with volume zero before any playback. If silence cannot be guaranteed, inspect metadata, frames and captions; mark playback unverified rather than starting sound. 6. Confirm byline, category/tags where applicable, stable canonical URL and served search metadata. Recheck relevant Rank Math flags after content changes, while keeping the plugin score separate from the article’s factual and visual pass. 7. Reconcile only the channels named in the distribution plan. Verify the direct Facebook/LinkedIn/YouTube links, group submission state and sent notifications as applicable. Repair in-scope failures and recheck affected output. If normal visitors still see stale content, use only the maintained authorized delivery procedure; record a blocker when that procedure fails rather than bypassing its checks. 9. Do not mark the entire article package complete while a required live check still fails. ## Required first-screen visual gate Every visitor-facing page, including home, money, relationship, archive and utility pages, must show a relevant authentic photograph, source-video poster or useful diagram above the fold. At 390x844 and 1280x800, test the anonymous unscrolled first visit with JavaScript on and off. A logo, social icon, decorative background, thin strip, broken image or empty player rectangle fails. The checker can measure a loaded photographic CSS background as well as images, diagrams and video posters. # Upload processed video to YouTube

Your finished video needs a place where people can watch it. This guide helps you upload it to the right channel and link it to the article. Start with the final file and the viewing plan for this job.

**The path:** Final source → Channel and details → Viewing state → Checked article pair.

**Use this when:** A source-checked edited video is ready for the brand’s YouTube channel under an agreed draft/private/unlisted/public/scheduled plan.

## Inputs
- The final video, rights, facts, source transcript and caption review state. Keep the source file/version identifiable.
- The exact channel and upload access through its approved account or role. Use [the channel setup task](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=set-up-youtube-channel-with-proper-branding#task-set-up-youtube-channel-with-proper-branding) only if this prerequisite is actually missing.
- The planned title, description, real thumbnail, relevant playlist and checked article URL if already public.
- The requested viewing state and any scheduled date/time/timezone, plus the article editor and content tracker.

## First-run prompt

> Use the final source file, exact channel and visibility plan I provide. Check for an existing upload, set accurate details, complete the already-authorized save/publication, and record the real ID and state. Keep preview checks silent and distinguish upload, processing, captions and article cross-links.

## Steps

# Enable YouTube captions by default

Captions help people follow a video with the sound off. This guide helps you set the player to show the captions it has. Start with the right video and check which caption tracks are really there.

**The path:** Verified video → Caption settings → Saved player → Silent visitor check.

**Use this when:** A page we control has a YouTube embed whose available captions should be requested by default.

## Inputs
- The correct video ID, page language and actual available caption-track evidence.
- The existing iframe (embedded player) or click-to-play facade, which is the poster/control that loads it. Include any VideoObject schema: the page’s machine-readable description of the video and its embed URL.
- The site’s supported source and edit authority. Check whether the maintained caption filter/helper already handles this embed.
- The page URL, accepted source revision and a way to perform silent desktop/mobile checks.

## First-run prompt

> Inspect the exact embed source and real video I provide. Use the existing supported filter/helper where it applies, set the documented caption and silent-first-load policy, and complete the authorized save. Check normal visitor output and real caption availability. Never invent an ID, track, quote, or playback result.

## Steps
1. Read the maintained [YouTube captions guide](https://blitzmetrics.com/youtube-captions-on-by-default/). Identify whether the current site uses its WordPress filter, a shared app helper, or a one-off iframe. Verify that mechanism exists and applies before relying on it; do not deploy a new fleet plugin for one page without that setup being in scope.
2. Confirm the video ID and page language from the real source. Inspect caption availability. A preferred language parameter does not create a caption track or prove that an automatic transcript is accurate.
3. Use the privacy-enhanced embed host `https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID`. Request `cc_load_policy=1` and `cc_lang_pref=en` or the actual page’s two-letter language code. Preserve other needed documented settings.
4. Keep `rel=0`, which limits related videos to the same channel rather than disabling them. Set `autoplay=0` or omit autoplay for the initial player. A future viewer click can load a player, but agent checks still must keep it muted at volume zero.
5. For an app facade, make its loaded player and VideoObject embed URL describe the same video and caption policy. They need not have byte-identical URLs when a documented click-only behavior differs. For a one-off iframe, put the intended parameters on its real src, not only a comment or data label.
6. Save through the supported source and complete an already-authorized publish/build. Read the saved output and the normal public URL. For a facade, inspect the player-building source as well as schema; schema alone does not prove the clicked player used the settings.
7. Check desktop and phone first load: no autoplay, right poster/player, readable controls and no overflow. Before any playback, verify mute and zero volume; otherwise inspect metadata/captions/stills and report the untested behavior.
8. Where silent playback is possible, check whether the intended real caption track appears. Record “parameters present; captions unavailable” if that is the truth. Keep player captions separate from the complete source transcript needed for quoting, then pass results to [Final formatting and QA checks](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=step-17-final-formatting-and-qa-checks#task-step-17-final-formatting-and-qa-checks).

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Correct video ID and page language are verified.
- [ ] The real player requests cc_load_policy=1 and the intended cc_lang_pref; privacy-enhanced host and rel=0 are present.
- [ ] First load does not autoplay, and all agent playback checks stay muted at zero volume.
- [ ] Saved source, built output and normal public result agree where applicable.
- [ ] Actual caption availability/behavior is recorded honestly; no track, quote evidence or playback pass is invented.

## Example(s)

**Teaching template — not a real video or tested player.** Replace `VIDEO_ID` with the verified source ID before use:

```text
https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/VIDEO_ID?autoplay=0&rel=0&cc_load_policy=1&cc_lang_pref=en
```

**Fictional teaching example:** a sample English page has a real video ID in its actual source, but that video has no caption track. The editor adds the intended parameters and verifies silent first load. The result is “settings saved; no captions available,” not “captions working.”

If the video later gets a checked track, test it again. Do not create an empty VTT file or treat player-generated words as a verified quotation. The template above must never be published with the literal `VIDEO_ID` placeholder.

The publisher gets the source revision, actual player URL, caption state and silent QA evidence. # Apply Metrics Decomposition

Your ad cost changed, but the total does not tell you why. This guide helps you break the result into clear parts. Start with the same goal and the numbers from each step.

**The path:** Top-line change → matching parts → likely driver → next check.

**Use this when:** A campaign’s cost or result changes and the team needs an evidence-backed explanation to guide the next action.

## Inputs
- Dated ad exports for the same goal and comparable periods, including spend, impressions, link clicks and counted results.
- Website visits/events only when they belong to that measured path; currency, time zone, attribution settings and tracking-change log.
- Written target and source definitions for each metric; read access and a calculation sheet are sufficient for this analysis.

## First-run prompt

> Break this changed result into matching components. Show units and arithmetic, reconcile the total where possible and label unmatched data. Distinguish a measured driver from a causal explanation. Return one useful next check with its owner; do not change campaigns from the analysis alone.

## Steps
1. Choose the goal’s actual top-line measure: cost per useful visit, qualified lead, sale or return on ad spend. Define what counts and keep different goal types separate.
2. Align account, period, time zone, currency and attribution scope. A platform conversion that includes view-through credit is not automatically part of a click-only site path. Record that mismatch before calculating.
3. For a consistently measured click path, collect spend, impressions, link clicks, landing-page visits and conversions. Keep missing counts unknown. A missing stage prevents full reconciliation; do not fill it from a different report just to get a zero residual.
4. Compute cost per thousand impressions (CPM), click rate (clicks ÷ impressions), visit rate (visits ÷ clicks) and conversion rate (conversions ÷ visits). Use rates as decimals in the identity: cost per conversion = CPM ÷ (1000 × click rate × visit rate × conversion rate). This works only when all counts describe the same path and denominators are nonzero.
5. Check the computed cost against spend ÷ matching conversions. Explain rounding, attribution or tracking differences instead of forcing agreement. For return on ad spend, use matched attributed revenue ÷ spend and keep profit separate.
6. Compare each component with the baseline. A lower click rate directs attention to the creative, offer or delivery mix; a weaker visit-to-conversion rate directs attention to the measured destination path. These are diagnostic leads, not proof of one cause.
7. Inspect the corresponding change log and evidence. Audience mix, auction conditions, site speed, consent, device mix and reporting lag can all matter. State a supported finding, a plausible explanation and what remains unknown separately.
8. Write the [Metrics, Analysis, and Action](https://blitzmetrics.com/maa/) line and name a specific next check or authorized repair. Preserve the worksheet so another reviewer can reproduce every number.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The chosen metric and each component have matching units and scope.
- [ ] Arithmetic handles missing or zero denominators without invented rates.
- [ ] Any residual or attribution mismatch is explained, not hidden.
- [ ] Measured changes and causal hypotheses are kept distinct.
- [ ] The next check has evidence, owner and an acceptance test.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example:** A test spends $100 for 10,000 impressions, 200 link clicks, 160 visits and eight matched leads. CPM is $10; the three rates are 0.02, 0.8 and 0.05. The formula gives $10 ÷ (1000 × 0.02 × 0.8 × 0.05) = $12.50 per lead, matching $100 ÷ 8. In a comparable period, only four leads occur with the same earlier counts, so cost becomes $25. The conversion stage changed. The next check is the form and offer evidence; the calculation alone does not prove the page caused the drop.

# Boost top 3–5 Facebook posts

Some of your posts helped people more than others. This guide helps you choose a few to test with a small ad budget. Start with the real posts and their recent results.

**The path:** Recent results → qualified short list → small tests → checked verdicts.

## Inputs

## First-run prompt

> Rank these Facebook posts against the Page’s comparable baseline. Pick up to three to five that fit the goal and have usable rights. Price each actual supported test and carry out only authorized actions. Return post/ad IDs, dates, cost and due review; do not fill the list with weak posts.

## Steps
1. Read the available 30-day organic log and disclose any shorter or missing history. Separate paid amplification from organic response. Compare like formats instead of ranking every post by raw reach.
2. Read shares, real questions, substantive comments and meaningful video metrics. Keep the goal in view: a funny post can be popular without helping the intended buyer.
3. Shortlist up to three to five posts with evidence and rights. Use fewer if fewer qualify. Preserve proof and relationship limits; a famous face or co-appearance alone does not support a client endorsement.
4. Choose relevant warm audiences first when they are eligible and fit the goal, as the source method recommends. A warm label does not prove enough people exist or make a mismatched audience right for the post.

6. Plan the nominal $1/day for seven days where supported. Price all rows and check true budget limits. A staged one-per-day sequence and a parallel batch have different overlapping commitments and due dates.
7. Launch only within the supplied scope, read back settings and monitor early delivery/ceiling errors. Preserve a stable full-window comparison while allowing protective actions already authorized.
8. At each due date, stop rows that fail the agreed rule and identify qualified winners. About 90% retirement is a portfolio expectation, not a forced quota. A winner can be considered for $30 total over 30 days or a separately bounded increase; neither happens automatically.

# Compare current vs last period performance

You want to know if this week went better than the last. This guide helps you compare the same kinds of results. Start with two clear time spans and the goal the work was meant to serve.

**The path:** Matched periods → checked changes → evidence limits → next-week report.

**Use this when:** A weekly or monthly promotion review is due, or the owner needs a fair before/after comparison.

## Inputs
- Current and prior source exports, matching metric definitions and the actual reporting goal.
- Exact dates, time zone, currency, campaign changes, outages and known reporting delay.
- Prior decisions and their actual execution evidence; read-only reporting access and the agreed report destination.

## First-run prompt

> Compare these periods using consistent definitions. Show absolute changes and percentages, handle zero baselines and note calendar or attribution limits. Treat the source’s 20% rule as a review flag, not proof of statistical significance. Return evidence-qualified findings and next actions without changing campaigns.

## Steps
1. Set exact current and prior dates. Prefer equal-length complete periods with comparable weekdays. Calendar months differ in length; show per-day measures or that limit if month-over-month reporting is required.
2. Use the same account, currency, time zone, metric definition and attribution window. Keep incomplete current periods or late conversion data labeled provisional; do not make them look like closed periods.
3. Compare the appropriate funnel measures: attention, useful engagement and actual business results. Separate spend, count, rate and cost. Do not add reach across overlapping channels as unique people.
4. For each metric, show prior value, current value, absolute change and relative change: (current − prior) ÷ prior. If the prior value is zero, the percentage is undefined; show the counts. For rates, distinguish percentage points from relative percent.
5. Use the source’s ±20% threshold as a triage flag alongside sample size, money and the goal. A 5% move can matter at scale; a 100% move from one to two results can be weak evidence. Neither threshold alone proves signal or noise.
6. Use [apply metrics decomposition](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=apply-metrics-decomposition#task-apply-metrics-decomposition) to locate the changed component, then consult the actual change log. Label causes verified, plausible or unknown. Do not force a cause onto every flagged row.
7. Separate supported improvements, deterioration, stable performance and unresolved evidence. A flat winner does not prove fatigue is coming. Check whether last period’s recommended action actually happened before crediting it.
8. Deliver the table through the already authorized report route, or save the report draft when delivery is outside scope. Give the next-week planner a small set of evidence-backed findings, with provisional data and due rechecks visible.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Dates and definitions are comparable or the precise limits are stated.
- [ ] Absolute, relative and percentage-point changes are correctly calculated.
- [ ] Zero baselines and incomplete periods are handled honestly.
- [ ] 20% flags are not called statistical proof or mandatory cause attribution.
- [ ] Actual actions and observed outcomes are separate in the report.

**Fictional teaching example:** A shop records 10 leads last week and 12 this week: two more, or a 20% rise. Spend rises from $100 to $144, so cost per lead rises from $10 to $12, also 20%. The report notes a holiday and no verified causal explanation, then names the next tracking and quality checks.

# Create and send Thank You Machine videos

Someone helped you, and you want to say thanks in a personal way. This guide helps you make a short video that names what they did. Start with the real moment and who should receive the message.

**The path:** Real moment → personal recording → scoped delivery → observed response.

**Use this when:** A verified referral, review, useful contribution or milestone deserves a personal acknowledgment.

## Inputs
- The exact person, factual trigger and appropriate destination, plus the scope for a private message, public post, tag or later reuse.
- The real speaker and recording device, approved facts/voice, and permission for any client details or third-party media.
- Access to the specific authorized sending/posting channel and a tracker for the recording, sent copy and any response. Paid promotion is separate scope.

## First-run prompt

> Prepare a brief thank-you from these facts: who helped, what they did and why it mattered. Have the actual speaker record it; do not invent their experience. Use only the authorized destination and send/share scope, verify any sent copy, and record the response as unknown until observed.

## Steps
1. Verify the trigger in its source record and choose the right recipient. Name a concrete contribution rather than generic praise. Do not call a person a client, mentor or close friend unless that relationship is supported.
2. Write a short recording brief with the person’s name, what happened, why it mattered and a sincere close. Aim for about a minute; do not force filler or invent business results to hit exactly 60 seconds.
3. Have the actual person record in their own voice. Keep it natural, with readable framing and a quiet setting. An agent can prepare the brief and process the file; it must not fabricate a human recording or first-person experience.
4. Check the file, captions and public/private details before delivery. Keep agent playback muted at volume zero. If spoken accuracy cannot be checked silently from a reliable transcript or by the speaker, record that review gap.
5. For an already authorized private send, verify the exact thread/recipient and send the agreed file or accessible link. Read back the sent copy. A prepared message, queued upload and delivered message are different states; do not resend from uncertainty alone.
6. Publish or tag the recipient only when that specific public use is in scope and the content is appropriate to share. A private thank-you does not automatically become public content. A recipient is free not to reply or reshare.
7. Consider derivatives only when useful, permissioned and authorized. Your thanks to someone is not their testimonial about your service. Any paid boost requires its own proven-content, audience and budget checks; it is not a mandatory part of saying thanks.
8. Save the trigger, actual recording, delivery state and any observed response. Route a future content idea or follow-up to its owner without manufacturing a testimonial, referral or new relationship claim.

- [ ] Trigger, recipient and relationship wording are supported by the source.
- [ ] The actual speaker’s recording and factual message are used.
- [ ] Private send, public post/tag, reuse and paid promotion each match existing scope.
- [ ] Any send/post has a read-back receipt; unknown response stays unknown.
- [ ] The result is not represented as a recipient endorsement or guaranteed referral.

**Fictional teaching example:** A shop owner thanks a volunteer who helped arrange a community repair day. The brief says exactly what the volunteer did and why it helped. # Create new saved audiences from Audience Insights

Your reports may show a group you have not served well yet. This guide helps you turn that clue into a clear test plan. Start with what the report can really show, not a guess about each person.

1. Open the exact current reports and note their source, date range and metric. Some demographics, interests or page affinities may not be available. Do not recreate a retired Audience Insights screen or infer individual identities from aggregate results.

4. Read the current controls and any automated expansion labels. A saved collection of suggestions is not an exact membership list. Keep warm/custom audience sources separate from a saved targeting preset.
5. Record a clear name and definition, such as service-area-topic-date, without embedding private customer names. Save the source report, settings, source rights and size/eligibility status. An estimate is not guaranteed delivery at $1/day.
6. If saving is authorized, create or update only the intended preset and read it back. Check for an existing equivalent before creating a duplicate. Keep active campaign targeting unchanged unless that distinct action is in scope.
7. Queue a proposal for a bounded switch test against an appropriate baseline. A preset may legitimately stay unused while budget, evidence or scope is pending; it is not a failed guide run because no ad launched.
8. Review prior test history before retiring a preset. Mark an outdated hypothesis or unavailable setting in the log; do not delete a shared audience used by active campaigns or declare a segment permanently bad from one weak test.

# Engage with social comments

People may ask good questions under your posts. This guide helps you reply with care and keep track of what needs more help. Start with the full thread so your answer fits what the person asked.

**The path:** Real thread → factual reply → scoped action → topic or handoff.

**Use this when:** An authorized comment review is due or a specific comment needs attention on a channel in scope.

## Inputs
- Access to the exact approved channels/posts and their complete comment threads, including existing replies.
- The owner’s factual voice guidance, approved offer/support information and scope for replies or moderation.
- Current support/escalation owner, moderation rules and a tracker for unresolved comments, useful questions and possible proof reuse.

## First-run prompt

> Review these exact comment threads, check for existing replies and prepare or post only responses already in scope. Answer from verified facts and the owner’s permitted voice. Keep private details out of public replies, preserve honest criticism and route unresolved issues to the real owner. Log questions without turning praise into an unapproved testimonial.

## Steps
1. Review only the named channels and recent/boosted posts in scope. Read the whole thread and check whether another worker already answered. Do not assume the source’s historical named group or every social account belongs in this job.
2. Classify each item: answerable question, useful feedback, support issue, abuse/spam or no reply needed. The source’s daily review and 24-hour response aim can guide an agreed service standard, but not every short comment needs an artificial question in return.
3. Use verified facts to answer the actual question in the owner’s permitted voice. Do not invent first-person experience, prices, delivery promises or relationships. A needed follow-up question should resolve the person’s need, not prolong the thread solely for engagement.
4. Post within existing reply authority and read back the exact comment. If approval or a source fact is genuinely missing, save the draft and name that narrow gap; do not demand approval again for already authorized routine replies.
5. Handle support details through the approved path without exposing customer records or requesting sensitive data publicly. Preserve honest criticism. Apply hiding/reporting/removal only under the actual moderation rule and authority, and record the reason.
6. Like or pin only when supported by the channel and appropriate within scope. These actions are not mandatory proof of a successful reply. Do not claim comment activity guarantees lower ad costs.
7. Capture recurring questions as topic ideas with source links. Treat praise as possible evidence requiring permission/context for reuse; a screenshot of a comment is not blanket permission to publish a testimonial everywhere.
8. Log what was answered, what remains open, response timing and the real next owner. Keep observed replies, referrals and ad metrics separate; do not attribute cost changes to the conversation without supporting evidence.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Every reviewed item has the correct thread and duplicate check.
- [ ] Replies are factual, useful and within the owner’s existing voice/action scope.
- [ ] Private details and honest criticism are handled under the real support/moderation policy.
- [ ] Posted actions have read-back; unanswered items have a reason and next owner.
- [ ] Topic/proof ideas remain distinct from approved reuse and claimed paid results.

**Fictional teaching example:** A viewer asks whether the seat-fix tip applies to a carbon frame. # Execute switch boost to target new audiences

A post has helped one group of people. You want to test whether it helps another group too. This guide helps you keep the post, cost and results clear as you try the next audience.

**The path:** Verified pair → new audience hypothesis → separate test → updated map.

**Use this when:** A Promote-stage post has a qualified result and an untested relevant audience is proposed.

## Inputs
- Original post/ad IDs, full-window result and cost target; the current audience/creative map.
- The proposed saved/custom audience definition, date, eligibility and actual service-area fit.
- Account roles, authorized new-test or replacement scope, total commitments, spend controls and start/end dates.

## First-run prompt

> Prepare the next audience test from this verified winning post. Preserve the original evidence and use the same eligible post where supported. Check whether this is an additional test or replacement, avoid duplicate launches, and act only within the supplied budget and action scope.

## Steps
1. Confirm the original pair met its stated goal with enough evidence for a new test. Keep its actual post, audience, metric, window and budget record available; a display name alone is not enough.
2. Read the proposed audience definition and source. A saved preset from the insights task is a hypothesis, not proof of future results. Check service-area fit, permissions and any suggestion/expansion behavior.
3. Choose a separate test by default when the plan is to preserve a still-running winner. If the authorized plan is a replacement, record the old stop and new start explicitly. Do not accidentally change the old audience and destroy the comparison record.
4. Use the existing post ID in a supported preview, preserving it where the platform allows. If a format or account requires a new creative, label that derivative and the comparison limit; do not promise social proof transfers everywhere.
5. Keep the creative and goal comparable while changing the planned audience variable. Use the method’s $1/day, seven-day idea only where accepted. Account for differing launch dates, overlap and auction delivery; it is not a randomized causal test.
6. Add old and new spending commitments before activation. Reconcile current worker state and existing ads so this Promote task and the related Dollar-a-Day task do not launch the same test twice.
7. Read back authorized saved/active settings, then check early delivery and budget safety. Keep the intended review window stable unless an agreed protective rule requires a change.
8. At the due date, compare the same cost and result definition with the baseline. Record keep, stop or bounded hold, update the audience/creative map, and name the next stage only when its conditions are met.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The winning pair and new hypothesis are source-backed and identifiable.
- [ ] Original evidence is preserved; any derivative or replacement is explicit.
- [ ] Actual budget controls, all commitments and dates fit scope.
- [ ] No duplicate test is created by overlapping recipes or retries.
- [ ] The updated map records the full result and its uncertainty.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example:** The Promote log has one seat-fix winner in Cedar Town. A new Maple Town preset is eligible and relevant. The operator finds that another worker already staged that exact post/audience test under the Dollar-a-Day recipe, so the Promote task reviews and completes that record rather than launching a duplicate. The map links one actual test to the parent campaign. It does not count two paid executions merely because two guide names describe the work.

## Handoff and Content Factory context

Qualified pairs can feed [sequence content cold warm conversion](https://local-service-spotlight.github.io/task-library/?task=sequence-content-cold-warm-conversion#task-sequence-content-cold-warm-conversion) or a reviewed budget decision.

# List top 3–5 recommendations for next 7 days

A report should help you choose what to do next. This guide turns the week’s findings into a short list of useful steps. Start with last week’s list and what really got done.

# Post roundup/listicle content

Your readers may need one place to find your best answers. This guide helps you turn strong past posts into a useful list. Start with one reader question and the pages that truly help answer it.

**The path:** Reader question → proven source pages → useful roundup → checked publication.

**Use this when:** A campaign or period has enough relevant published source material for a reader-focused roundup.

## Inputs
- Exact published source URLs and dated evidence of their usefulness; rights to images, clips and excerpts.
- The reader question, existing topic hub and [SEO Tree](https://blitzmetrics.com/seo-tree/) placement so the roundup has a distinct job.
- Current [Article Guidelines](https://localservicespotlight.com/article-guidelines/), the actual CMS/save rail, author/category requirements, publication scope and any named distribution channels.

## First-run prompt

> Build a helpful roundup for this reader question from the supplied verified pages. Keep the topic hub authoritative, use meaningful owned links and check media rights. Publish only through the supported existing CMS rail when authorized, then verify the canonical page at desktop and phone sizes. Distribution and paid promotion must match their own existing scope.

## Steps
1. Choose the exact question the roundup answers and check existing pages first. Update an appropriate existing roundup when it serves the same job; do not create a competing definitive page or rename a source hub to make room.
2. Select the strongest relevant source pieces using the period’s actual evidence. The source suggests five to ten, but use only as many as the question warrants. Different metrics serve different goals; traffic alone does not prove qualified business impact.
3. For each item, read the full source and write a brief takeaway that helps the reader decide whether to open it. Link with descriptive text to the maintained owned leaf or guide. Preserve primary external proof when needed instead of replacing evidence with a vague internal link.
4. Place a clear grade-5 opening and a meaningful photo or diagram in the first desktop and phone screen. Each item needs useful visual context when it aids understanding, with accurate captions, alt text and rights. Keep video embeds silent during checks and captions available.
5. Tie the roundup to its parent branch and relevant included leaves through the [SEO Tree](https://blitzmetrics.com/seo-tree/). Explain methods on their maintained owned pages at first mention. Do not add every sibling or turn the roundup into a wall of unrelated links.
6. Review factual and relationship claims against their sources. A name, image or mention does not establish endorsement. Do not turn a selected example into a task recipe or certify an article merely because it appears in this roundup.
7. Use the actual supported CMS pipeline for the existing type and builder. Preserve canonical URL, Page/Post identity and durable save source. Apply the maintained editorial checks; plugin scores and automatic link suggestions do not replace semantic and visual review.
8. When authorized, publish and read back the saved source, then the ordinary canonical URL. Check links, readable first-screen content, media and phone/desktop overflow. Share only to named channels in scope, then measure the roundup’s own response before treating it as a paid winner.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] The reader question and distinct SEO Tree role are clear.
- [ ] Each selected source was read and linked with relevant descriptive text.
- [ ] Opening, meaningful lead visual, captions and claims meet current standards.
- [ ] Publication preserves the supported CMS type, source and canonical URL.
- [ ] Actual public read-back and channel receipts are separate from saved drafts and future boost eligibility.

**Fictional teaching example:** A shop has three strong articles on loose seats, brake checks and tire wear. A simple three-part inspection diagram leads the page. The site has an existing Page built with its supported builder, so the operator updates that source rather than converting it to a Post. # Review budget allocation by channel

Your ad money may be spread across several places. This guide helps you see what each one cost and what it did. Start with the goal and the real spend for the same time span.

**The path:** Matched spend → comparable results → bounded proposal → measured recheck.

**Use this when:** A campaign budget review is due or spending no longer appears aligned with the stated goal.

## Inputs
- Dated spend and result exports by channel/campaign with currency, attribution and result definitions.
- The actual total budget, commitments, targets and stage roles; margin/revenue evidence when return is part of the goal.
- Prior allocation decisions, current operator authority and any limits on changes, stops or new tests. Read access is enough to prepare the review.

## First-run prompt

> Reconcile spend and compare each line with its matching goal. Separate cost targets from return targets and preserve attribution limits. Propose a bounded before/after allocation, keeping uncommitted funds unspent unless their use is authorized. Execute only changes already in scope and record actual read-back.

## Steps
1. Build a table by channel and campaign with spend, result count, definition, matching cost or return, target and stage. Reconcile totals to source reports, avoiding double-counted campaign/ad-set subtotals.
2. Keep currencies and windows consistent. Do not add each platform’s attributed conversions as unique business sales without a supported reconciliation. Keep paid, organic and blended measures explicitly separate.
3. Compare like goals. For cost per acquisition, above the target is worse; for return on ad spend, below the target is worse. A cheap view is not a cheaper lead, and revenue divided by spend is not profit.
4. Check result quality, tracking and minimum evidence before labeling a winner. An ad at its budget limit is not automatically underfunded, and an expensive qualified sale can be more useful than cheap irrelevant leads.
5. Review stage coverage against the actual plan and eligible audiences. A full nurture program may need several jobs, but every account need not fund all stages or all platforms. A stage can remain unfunded when evidence, audience size or scope does not support it.
6. Create a before/after proposal with each change’s reason, amount, dates and recheck. Preserve the small-test method and ≤2× ceiling for any separate increases, without claiming platform learning is guaranteed safe. Consider the current $30 total/30-day continuation before assuming vertical increases.
7. Keep any research reserve tied to actual authority and proven-content rules. The old roughly-10% language is not permission to divert money into unproven ads. Stopped spend stays uncommitted unless a specific reallocation is covered.
8. Apply only authorized exact changes and read them back; otherwise deliver the proposal through the existing route. Record what really changed and the next measurement window so the following report can judge the decision.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Spend totals reconcile without duplicate subtotals or mixed currencies.
- [ ] Cost and return goals use the correct direction and matched result type.
- [ ] Quality/attribution gaps prevent unsupported winner labels.
- [ ] The proposal fits real totals, stages, dates and change authority.
- [ ] Proposed, applied and observed effects are separately documented.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example:** Two channels spend $100 each. A produces five qualified leads, or $20 per lead. B produces ten, or $10 per lead, against a $15 target. A’s source quality is checked before a stop is proposed. B is a candidate for a further bounded test, not proof that twice the spend will buy twice the leads. Separately, a sales campaign has a 4× return target but records 3×, so it misses the target even though the number is “below target.” Unspent money is not moved without the existing scope covering that change.

You have posts that people already find useful. This guide helps you test them with a small ad budget and learn from the results. Start with the proof, the goal and the total you can spend.

**The path:** Qualified content → priced tests → due verdicts → next bounded cycle.

## First-run prompt

1. Read each post and give it a primary job: introduce why it matters, explain how the work helps, or offer a relevant next action. The owned WHY/HOW/WHAT method is useful context; do not force a piece into a stage solely from its title.
2. Build the content map with the source URL, stage, intended audience, result and actual next link. Missing proof or offer material remains a production gap; do not invent case studies to fill a sequence.

# Set up remarketing ads for landing page abandoners

Some people leave your site before they ask for help. A useful follow-up may answer what they still need to know. This guide helps you check who can be reached and whether a small test makes sense.

**The path:** Checked visit signal → eligible audience → useful follow-up → measured result.

**Use this when:** A defined landing page has eligible visitor data and the campaign proposes a bounded follow-up test.

## Inputs
- Exact landing page and actual conversion definition, including confirmed event or destination rather than assuming a thank-you URL.
- The selected platform’s tracking and audience source, permissions, consent/policy requirements and current eligibility.
- Approved follow-up creative, goal/target, supported budget controls, total amount and dates; actual campaign setup authority.

## First-run prompt

> Check whether this landing-page visitor follow-up is feasible. Define visit and conversion-exclusion rules, read actual audience eligibility and select a relevant time window. Use only the platforms and budget already in scope. Do not broaden a too-small audience or call every visitor an identified lost customer.

## Steps
1. Define the audience honestly: people with the recorded visit signal and no recorded conversion under the chosen rule. Some may have converted offline or through an unmeasured path; “abandoner” is a measurement label, not knowledge of each person’s intent.
2. Check the actual visit and conversion event path under [Digital Plumbing](https://blitzmetrics.com/digital-plumbing/). A confirmed conversion event can support exclusion without a separate thank-you page. Installing a Meta pixel is not a universal prerequisite for a Google-only plan.
3. Use only the selected platform and permitted data source. Follow its actual consent, eligibility and restricted-offer rules. Google’s website-audience rules support included and excluded actions; do not upload or expose private customer records to fill a gap.
4. Choose a membership window that matches the offer’s buying cycle and the campaign plan. One day is a short recency-test option from the source, not a universal cutoff after which all intent is gone. Record the exclusion duration and any expected reporting lag.
5. Read the audience’s real serving eligibility. Google’s current guide uses active-user requirements that differ from raw analytics visitor counts; a small one-day group may not be able to serve. An insufficient group stays pending unless the existing scope supports a different relevant window or plan.
6. Choose proof or an answer that addresses a real unresolved question, with rights and claim checks. Avoid personal wording that implies you know an individual visited the page. Do not assume a testimonial is always the right follow-up.
7. For a feasible authorized test, set the actual platform budget level and dates, including all commitments. Google budgets are campaign-level. Read back inclusion/exclusion, any audience expansion and the budget before calling it a remarketing-only test.
8. Check early delivery and frequency, then review matched cost and useful outcomes against the goal. Remarketing is not guaranteed to be the cheapest channel. If it performs poorly, inspect tracking, audience, offer and delivery evidence before blaming the page or automatically rotating creative.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Visit/no-recorded-conversion rules and their limits are documented.
- [ ] Platform-specific tracking, data rights and actual eligibility pass or remain pending.
- [ ] Window and converter exclusion fit the buying cycle and supported controls.
- [ ] Budget, dates and audience-only claims match saved settings.
- [ ] The result is measured against the goal without guaranteed cheapest-conversion or causal claims.

**Fictional teaching example:** A shop’s quote page has 12 eligible recorded visitors in a day, but the selected Google audience does not meet the current serving requirement. # Add Schema Markup (Person/LocalBusiness)

Search tools can mix up a person and a business. This guide helps a site owner add a small fact record to the page. Start with facts and profile links that you can prove.

**The path:** Proven facts → Right entity → Page record → Validation.

**Use this when:** a site lacks structured facts, has conflicting entity records, or changes its public business information.

## Inputs
- The canonical public name, page URL, entity type and verified same-entity profile links. Keep private addresses and personal contact details out unless approved for publication.
- The existing structured-data output and its owner: SEO plugin, theme or code. Access only to the source needed for this change.
- Public page content that supports each proposed fact and the search feature, if any, that you intend to support.

## First-run prompt

> Read the existing page and structured records. Add or correct the actual person or business entity using supported facts and the current owning source. Keep distinct entities separate. Validate syntax and any applicable Google feature without promising a Knowledge Panel or rich result.

## Steps
1. Read the visible page and all existing JSON-LD, microdata or plugin output. List existing entity IDs so a new record will not create a second conflicting business.
2. Choose the right entity: Person for an individual, an appropriate LocalBusiness type for an eligible local business, or Organization when that better fits. A founder and their company are separate records, connected only by a true stated relationship.
3. Build a fact table with value, public source and entity. Define `sameAs` as a link that identifies this same person or business. A news mention or a person’s employer page is not automatically the same entity.
4. Edit the current owning plugin or code field. Use a stable URL-based identifier and absolute public URLs. Include only supported properties; an invented job title, street address or rating is not a way to satisfy a validator.
5. For a relevant Google feature, read that feature’s current required and recommended fields. Generic Person markup is not itself a promise of a supported rich-result feature. Keep non-applicable recommendations separate from real errors.
6. Save the change through the supported publishing route. Read the ordinary public page and compare the served record with the intended values, including correct characters and valid JSON.
7. Validate syntax and entity relationships, then use Google’s Rich Results Test only for applicable features. Inspect warnings individually and fix factual or syntax defects at the source. “No supported item detected” is not proof that generic schema is invalid.
8. Check representative templates for duplicate or stale records and visible facts that disagree. Save the final entity IDs, public URLs, validator results and remaining search-feature limits.

## Definition of done (QA checklist)

- [ ] Each record represents the correct entity and agrees with visible, supported facts.
- [ ] Same-entity profile links are separated from relationship and reference links.
- [ ] JSON parses and no conflicting duplicate entity has been added.
- [ ] Applicable validation errors are resolved; non-applicable feature results are labeled accurately.
- [ ] Public read-back and the owning source are recorded; no ranking or Knowledge Panel outcome is claimed.

## Example(s)

**Fictional teaching example.** A workshop site describes an owner named Lee Hart and the company Oak Repair. A minimal business record is `{"@context":"https://schema.org","@type":"LocalBusiness","@id":"https://example.com/#business","name":"Oak Repair","url":"https://example.com/"}`. A separate Person record holds Lee’s facts. The company’s LinkedIn Page belongs with the business; Lee’s personal profile belongs with the Person. This teaches record identity and valid JSON. # Claim and Brand Facebook Page

People may find an old or wrong Page when they search for your business. This guide helps you fix the right Facebook Page. Start by finding the Page your business should own and checking who can edit it.

**The path:** Find Page → Check control → Update facts → Public check.

**Use this when:** a business needs a Page, has an unclaimed listing, or needs its existing Page brought into line with current facts.

## Inputs
- The business identity record, canonical website and any existing Page IDs or URLs.
- A legitimate account with the needed Page permissions, or the actual owner who can provide them. Record access without sharing passwords.
- Rights-cleared logo, cover photo, business description, public contact details and the requested scope of changes.

## First-run prompt

> Find the existing business Page before creating one. Verify access and the real business facts, then complete authorized branding edits. Report pending access separately from public branding. Do not merge Pages, transfer control, send invitations or run ads unless those actions are included in the job.

## Steps
1. Search the known Page URL, business name and location. Record likely matches and why each is the same business or a distinct valid location, brand or person. Multiple results do not prove that they should be merged.
2. Open the actual Page management view and confirm the Page ID and current role. Meta distinguishes Facebook access from task access, and full control can manage permissions. An invitation or request is pending until accepted and usable.
3. If no Page exists, use Meta’s supported create-Page flow for the real business. If one exists but access is missing, use the supported request or owner-grant route within current authority. Keep a named dependency for missing control; do not create a competing Page as a shortcut.
4. Update the public business name, category, website and contact details from the identity record. Select an available clear handle. Preserve service-area address privacy and supported platform formatting rather than forcing identical characters everywhere.
5. Add the approved logo and cover image, checking crop and legibility on phone and desktop. Use real owned or licensed material; a fictional staff photo or implied customer endorsement does not belong on a real Page.
6. Write a short About section that says what the business does, whom it serves and how to reach it. Company voice may use “we”; do not force a company to speak as one individual or invent claims.
7. Choose an appropriate contact action supported by this Page and test its destination without sending an unrequested message. Link a business portfolio or Instagram account only when that connection serves the agreed workflow; do not create an ad account just for branding.

- [ ] Public branding and private account-control evidence are recorded separately.

name: configure-https-with-no-mixed-content

# Configure HTTPS With No Mixed Content

A browser warning can stop a buyer from using your site. This guide helps a site owner fix secure page links and the files they load. Start with the site’s real host and the web addresses people use.

**The path:** Known host → Valid certificate → Secure files → Public checks.

**Use this when:** a site launches, moves hosts, changes domains, or reports certificate or mixed-content warnings.

## Inputs
- The actual host, content delivery service, canonical hostname and required aliases, with supported access for the planned changes.
- The current certificate and renewal configuration, redirect rules and a recoverable before state.
- A representative page list including forms, images, downloads and login paths; the CMS’s actual installation and public URL settings.

## First-run prompt

> Inspect the requested hostnames and their HTTPS setup. Fix supported certificate, redirect or mixed-resource defects in scope, preserving paths and working features. Validate normal public URLs and report renewal configuration separately from future renewal proof.

## Steps
1. List the intended public hostname and aliases actually used by visitors or existing links. Capture current DNS, certificate coverage and redirects. Do not invent extra hostnames or change nameservers for this task.
2. Use the host’s supported certificate flow for those names. Verify the certificate is trusted, covers the names and is valid now. Check the actual renewal job or managed-service setting; a model or a hosting brand alone does not prove renewals will run.
3. Set HTTP-to-HTTPS redirection at the existing owning layer. Preserve the intended path and query, and avoid loops between the edge and origin. A supported permanent redirect may use 301 or 308. Do not add HSTS preload as an unrequested side effect.
4. Check CMS public URL and installation URL settings against the real architecture. They need not be identical when WordPress is installed in a subdirectory. Use the supported source update and backup procedure instead of a blind text replacement in stored database data.
5. Inspect loaded subresources on key pages. Update owned image, script, stylesheet and embed references to working HTTPS endpoints. Ordinary outbound HTTP navigation is a different issue from insecure resources loaded inside an HTTPS page.
6. For a third-party resource without secure support, replace or remove it only within the page’s approved scope and preserve necessary functionality. Do not bypass certificate checks or weaken browser security to hide the failure.
7. Read the normal public pages with network and console evidence. Check for blocked or auto-upgraded insecure resources, and confirm forms, media controls and images still work. Keep all media silent.
8. Verify relevant public redirects again and save final evidence. Check the existing Search Console property scope: a Domain property covers protocols; a URL-prefix property is more specific. Add a new property only if the actual measurement setup needs it.

- [ ] Required hostnames have valid trusted certificates and correct canonical redirects.
- [ ] No unintended insecure subresource request remains on the checked pages.
- [ ] Paths, queries, forms and meaningful media survive the changes.
- [ ] Renewal configuration and rollback location are documented without claiming an unobserved future renewal.
- [ ] Public URL, time, representative page coverage and any untested host or feature are recorded.
